themes.title: Birds
themes.hook: Watch them, give them water, become one.

activities.title: Watch the birds
activities.oneLiner: Ten quiet minutes noticing who is out there.
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing but a spot to sit with a view of some trees, a garden, or the street. A cushion each if you like.
activities.getReady: Pick your spot before you start so you can settle in quietly. Early morning or late afternoon is best. A bird chart or app can sit nearby, but don't lead with it.
activities.howToDoIt: Sit close together and watch. Count how many you see. Notice the colours, the sounds, and the way each one moves. You might spot a rainbow lorikeet, a magpie, a willie wagtail or a rosella, or hear a kookaburra.
activities.howToGuide: Be still and watch alongside them rather than talking the whole time. Follow their pointing. Don't turn it into a quiz on names.
activities.trySaying: "I wonder what that one's looking for."
activities.ifNotWorking: No birds about? Close your eyes and count the calls you can hear instead, or look up which birds live in your area and hunt for one tomorrow.
activities.makeEasier: For a younger one, the whole game is just "can you spot a bird?" One is a win.
activities.makeHarder: For an older one, name three different birds, or watch one and guess what it's doing.
activities.builds: The kind of focus that holds on something slow and quiet.
activities.whyItWorks: Birds give no instant reward, so watching them grows attention the exact opposite way a screen shrinks it.
activities.downTheTrack: The child who can watch a bird can later sit with a hard book.
activities.safety: Australian magpies can swoop to protect their nests in spring, roughly August to November. Wonderful birds, just keep a friendly distance from any nest and watch from further back at that time of year.

activities.title: Make a bird bath
activities.oneLiner: The kind, Aussie way to bring birds to your place.
activities.whatYouNeed: A shallow dish or old plant-pot saucer. A handful of small stones. Fresh water. A shady spot, up off the ground if you can, near cover but with a clear view.
activities.getReady: Have the dish, stones and water together so it's a smooth little job.
activities.howToDoIt: They place a few stones in the dish so small birds and bees have somewhere to stand. Fill it with a few centimetres of water. Set it in its spot together. Then over the coming days, watch who visits. We give birds water, never food.
activities.howToGuide: Let their hands do the placing and pouring, even though it's slower. The first bird to use their bath is a big moment.
activities.trySaying: "You made somewhere safe for the birds. Let's see who finds it."
activities.ifNotWorking: It can take days or even weeks for birds to find it. Put it where you already see birds, and keep it topped up. Patience is half the lesson.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just fills and places it.
activities.makeHarder: An older child keeps it clean and topped up as their own real job.
activities.builds: Patience, and caring for living things the right way.
activities.whyItWorks: The making is hands-on and the reward is late and uncertain, and keeping it clean is a real weekly job.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking at things that take time, and real care for the world around them.
activities.safety: Water, not food, is what BirdLife Australia and most councils recommend, because bread, seed and cereal make native birds sick. Change the water every day or two, scrub the dish weekly, and keep it where the cat can't lie in wait.

activities.title: Be a bird
activities.oneLiner: Nest, flap, and carry on like a kookaburra.
activities.whatYouNeed: A few cushions and a blanket for a nest. A bit of room to move.
activities.getReady: Clear a small space so nobody bumps a coffee table mid-flight.
activities.howToDoIt: Build a nest together, then become birds. Flap, hop, and act out a whole bird's day. Try real Aussie sounds, a kookaburra's laugh, a magpie's warble, a cockatoo's screech. Feed your baby birds, fly off for water, come home to the nest.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their story rather than running it. If the birds also drive a bus today, the birds drive a bus. Join in as another bird.
activities.trySaying: "What does our bird do next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Shy about the sounds? Start it yourself and be a bit silly. Once you've done the kookaburra laugh, they'll want a turn.
activities.makeEasier: Just the flapping and the nest is enough for a little one.
activities.makeHarder: An older child acts out a proper story, a storm, finding food, a baby learning to fly.
activities.builds: Imagination, and stepping into someone else's shoes.
activities.whyItWorks: Becoming a bird is the same mental move as imagining how another creature feels.
activities.downTheTrack: Making new things, and reading how other people feel.
activities.safety: Big feelings can come out in pretend play, and that's healthy. If it gets too wild, land the birds in the nest for a rest.

activities.title: Draw the bird you saw
activities.oneLiner: Put the bird you spotted onto paper, your own way.
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, and whatever makes marks, crayons, textas or pencils.
activities.getReady: If you did the watching activity, talk about the bird you saw first. Otherwise find a photo of a common local bird to look at together, a magpie, a lorikeet or a willie wagtail.
activities.howToDoIt: Draw the bird together. Not a perfect bird, their bird. Look at the real shape. Is the body round or long? What colour is it? A long tail or a fat little beak? Let them lead, and draw your own alongside.
activities.howToGuide: Resist drawing it for them. Ask what they can see rather than telling them what a bird looks like. Every wobbly bird is theirs, and that matters more than neat.
activities.trySaying: "What did your bird look like? Let's put that bit in."
activities.ifNotWorking: If they say they can't do it, start with one circle for the body and let them add from there. Or you draw the outline and they colour it in.
activities.makeEasier: A younger one might scribble a colour and call it a bird. Perfect.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds the feet, the eye, a background, or draws the bird doing something.
activities.builds: Looking hard at something real, then making your own version of it.
activities.whyItWorks: Copying a cartoon trains nothing. Drawing a bird they actually watched makes them study the real thing, then decide how to show it.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing detail others miss, and turning what they see into something of their own.
activities.safety: Drawing from something real, rather than copying a cartoon, is where close looking and imagination meet. There is no wrong bird here.

activities.title: Build a nest from the garden
activities.oneLiner: Can you make a home a bird would be proud of?
activities.whatYouNeed: A handful of natural bits from the garden or a park, dry grass, small twigs, leaves, and any feathers you find. A shallow bowl, or just a patch of ground.
activities.getReady: Head out together and gather the materials first. Make the gathering part of it, it's half the fun.
activities.howToDoIt: Try to build a nest that holds together, the way a bird would. Weave and tuck the twigs, line it with soft grass and leaves. Test it. Does it hold? Would an egg roll out? Fix the gaps together.
activities.howToGuide: Let them problem-solve when it falls apart, that's the whole point. Ask what a bird might do rather than fixing it yourself. The wobbles are where the thinking happens.
activities.trySaying: "It keeps falling apart there. What could we use to hold it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If it won't hold at all, start with the bowl as a base and build the nest inside it. A win they can see keeps them going.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just piles the soft things into a bowl. That's a nest.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds it freestanding, no bowl, strong enough to hold a small stone "egg".
activities.builds: Working a real problem with your hands until it holds together.
activities.whyItWorks: A nest that keeps collapsing is a puzzle with no single answer, so they have to try, watch what fails, and try again.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with a hard job instead of giving up, and thinking like a maker.
activities.safety: Never take a real nest or eggs, and leave any wild nest well alone. This is about building your own from loose bits on the ground.

activities.title: Name a bird for every letter
activities.oneLiner: A gentle game of how many birds do we know.
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing at all. Perfect for the car, the bath, or waiting anywhere.
activities.getReady: None. This one travels with you.
activities.howToDoIt: Go through the alphabet and try to name a bird for each letter. Laugh about the tricky ones. Look a few up together when you get stuck, that's part of it.
activities.howToGuide: Keep it playful, not a test. Wrong guesses are great, they're a chance to wonder together. Let them surprise you with ones they know.
activities.trySaying: "Hmm, what bird starts with a K? I can hear one in the mornings."
activities.ifNotWorking: Too hard for a little one? Just count how many birds you can name between you, no letters. Or stick to A, B and C.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child names any birds they know while you find the letters.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds where each bird lives, or one thing it does.
activities.builds: A growing store of real knowledge, and the urge to fill the gaps.
activities.whyItWorks: Reaching for a bird per letter makes them dig through what they know and notice what they don't, which is where looking-it-up begins.
activities.downTheTrack: Loving to know things, and knowing the difference between a guess and a fact.
activities.safety: This is quietly building a store of real knowledge, and the habit of looking things up rather than guessing.

themes.bringItTogether: Sit with them at the end and ask what surprised them about birds today.

themes.title: Water
themes.hook: Pour it, test it, paint with it.

activities.title: The pouring station
activities.oneLiner: How much fits before it spills?
activities.whatYouNeed: A few plastic cups and jugs of different sizes, a large tray or the kitchen sink, a tea towel for spills.
activities.getReady: Set the cups on the tray and half fill one jug. Roll up sleeves. Put the tea towel where it can be grabbed fast.
activities.howToDoIt: Let them pour water from cup to cup and jug to jug. Watch what happens when a small cup fills a big one, and when a big one overflows a small one.
activities.howToGuide: Hold back from steadying their hands. Let a spill happen and let them mop it. Ask what they think will fit before they pour.
activities.trySaying: "Will all of that fit in the little cup?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If pouring is too hard, start with a small jug that is easy to lift and only a little water inside.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child scoops and tips with one cup. That is plenty.
activities.makeHarder: An older one fills a jug to an exact line, or pours three cups into one without a spill.
activities.builds: Steady hands and a feel for how much a container holds.
activities.whyItWorks: Pouring gives instant, honest feedback, so they adjust their aim and speed every single try.
activities.downTheTrack: Trusting their own hands to do a real job, which no screen can teach.
activities.safety: Never leave a child alone with water, even a shallow tray. Tip it out the moment you finish.

activities.title: Sink or float
activities.oneLiner: Which things ride on top, and which go straight down?
activities.whatYouNeed: A big bowl or tub of water, a handful of safe household bits like a cork, a spoon, a leaf, a plastic lid, a grape, a coin, a peg.
activities.getReady: Fill the tub. Gather the objects in a pile beside it. Have a towel underneath.
activities.howToDoIt: Before each object goes in, ask them to guess sink or float. Then drop it in and watch. Sort the objects into two piles as you go.
activities.howToGuide: Let them be wrong and stay curious. Do not correct the guess, let the water do it. Then ask why they think the heavy spoon sank but the big lid did not.
activities.trySaying: "You guessed float. Let's see if the water agrees."
activities.ifNotWorking: If every guess is a shrug, start with two very different things, a cork and a coin, so the pattern is clear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just drops things in and watches, no guessing needed.
activities.makeHarder: An older one tests whether a lump of foil sinks, then whether the same foil shaped into a boat floats.
activities.builds: Making a prediction and checking it against what really happens.
activities.whyItWorks: A guess that turns out wrong is the best kind, because it makes them look harder next time.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling a real result from a good guess, the root of clear thinking.
activities.safety: Keep grapes and coins away from the mouth, they are choking hazards. Stay within arm's reach of the water the whole time.

activities.title: Paint the path with water
activities.oneLiner: A giant brush, a bucket, and a wall to cover.
activities.whatYouNeed: A bucket of water and a big paintbrush, a roller, or an old sponge. A dry fence, path, or brick wall.
activities.getReady: Fill the bucket outside. Pick a dry surface where the water marks will show up dark. Pop hats on if the sun is out.
activities.howToDoIt: Dip and paint. Make big shapes, letters, a face, a wobbly snake. Then watch the marks fade as they dry and paint them again.
activities.howToGuide: Let them lead the picture. Notice the fading with them rather than rushing to redo it. Ask what they want to paint before the last one disappears.
activities.trySaying: "The sun is drinking your painting. What will you make next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If the surface dries too fast to see, move to shade or a darker brick where the wet mark lasts longer.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child slaps water about with a sponge and calls it done.
activities.makeHarder: An older one races the sun to finish a whole word before the first letter vanishes.
activities.builds: Making bold marks freely, with nothing to clean up and no way to get it wrong.
activities.whyItWorks: Water that vanishes takes the pressure off, so they paint again and again without fear of a mess.
activities.downTheTrack: The nerve to make something, watch it go, and start fresh.
activities.safety: Slip, slop, slap if you are out in the sun. A hat and sunscreen even on cool days, as Australian sun is strong most of the year.

activities.title: The great ice rescue
activities.oneLiner: A toy is frozen in a block. Can you free it?
activities.whatYouNeed: A small plastic toy, a container, water, a freezer. Later, a cup of warm water, a spoon, and some salt.
activities.getReady: The day before, sit the toy in the container, cover with water, and freeze it overnight. Turn the block out when you are ready.
activities.howToDoIt: Set the ice block in a tray and work out how to free the toy. Trickle warm water on it, sprinkle salt, tap it gently, or just hold it and wait.
activities.howToGuide: This is a slow job, so let them feel the wait. Do not crack it open for them. Ask which trick is melting it fastest.
activities.trySaying: "It's taking a while. What's helping it melt quickest?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If patience runs out, pour on warmer water to speed the rescue and keep spirits up.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child holds the block in warm hands over the tray and watches it shrink.
activities.makeHarder: An older one freezes two blocks and tests which melts first, one with salt and one without.
activities.builds: Staying with a slow task and trying more than one way through.
activities.whyItWorks: Ice will not be hurried, so they learn that effort plus time gets the job done.
activities.downTheTrack: Patience for problems that do not solve in a second.
activities.safety: Warm water, never hot, as small hands scald easily. Never use a knife or anything sharp to chip the ice.

activities.title: Music in the glasses
activities.oneLiner: Fill them up and play a tune.
activities.whatYouNeed: Four or five sturdy glasses or jars, water, a metal spoon.
activities.getReady: Line the glasses up and fill each to a different level, from a splash to nearly full. Set them on a steady bench.
activities.howToDoIt: Tap each glass softly with the spoon and listen. The fuller ones sound low, the emptier ones sound high. Add or tip out water to change the note, then play a little tune.
activities.howToGuide: Let them tap and listen before you explain anything. Ask them to close their eyes and pick the high glass from the low one by ear.
activities.trySaying: "Listen. Which glass sings the highest?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If the taps all sound the same, spread the water levels wider so the difference is easy to hear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just taps and listens, no tune needed.
activities.makeHarder: An older one tunes the glasses to match a simple song like Twinkle Twinkle.
activities.builds: Ears that pick out small differences in sound.
activities.whyItWorks: Changing the water changes the note right away, linking what they do to what they hear.
activities.downTheTrack: Close listening, the kind that reads a room and not just a screen.
activities.safety: More water means a slower, lower ring. Less water rings higher and faster. Use glasses, not fine crystal, so a firm tap does no harm.

activities.title: Give the toys a bath
activities.oneLiner: A muddy toy, a warm tub, and a job to do.
activities.whatYouNeed: A tub of warm soapy water, a cloth or soft brush, some grubby plastic or bath toys, a towel.
activities.getReady: Half fill the tub with warm water and a little dish soap. Lay the towel out ready for the clean, wet toys.
activities.howToDoIt: Wash each toy with care. Scrub the mud from the wheels, wipe the face, rinse it, and lay it on the towel to dry. Treat each one like it matters.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide the order and how clean is clean. Talk about looking after the things we love. Ask which toy needs the most help today.
activities.trySaying: "This little one is covered in mud. Shall we look after it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If they lose interest, give one toy a name and a story about how it got so dirty.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child dunks and swishes one toy in the tub.
activities.makeHarder: An older one runs a proper wash line, one tub to scrub and one to rinse, and dries each toy before the next.
activities.builds: Caring for something and following a job through to dry and done.
activities.whyItWorks: A small creature in their care pulls out gentleness and pride in doing it right.
activities.downTheTrack: The habit of tending things and people, which stays valuable whatever else changes.
activities.safety: Warm, not hot, water and never a child left alone by the tub. Tip it out as soon as you are done.

themes.bringItTogether: Across a week of these, your child pours with steady hands, tests a guess against real water, and learns that some jobs just take time.

themes.title: Shadows
themes.hook: Catch them, chase them, tell a story with them.

activities.title: Catch your own shadow
activities.oneLiner: Can you stand on it, or make it hide?
activities.whatYouNeed: A sunny day and an open space, a path, backyard, or park.
activities.getReady: Head out when the sun is out. Find a clear patch of ground where shadows fall long and easy to see.
activities.howToDoIt: Find your shadow and try to jump on it, stamp on its head, or make it wave. Then try to hide it by standing in shade, and find it again in the sun.
activities.howToGuide: Let them puzzle over why the shadow will not be caught. Move together into shade and back and ask where it went.
activities.trySaying: "Try to stand on your shadow's head. Can you?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If shadows are faint, try mid morning or late afternoon when the sun is low and shadows stretch long.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just waves and watches the dark shape copy them.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plays shadow tag, tagging a friend by stepping on their shadow instead of their body.
activities.builds: Noticing how their own body throws a shape they can chase.
activities.whyItWorks: A shadow that dodges every stamp turns a simple idea into a game they keep testing.
activities.downTheTrack: Paying close attention to how the real world behaves.
activities.safety: Slip, slop, slap for time outdoors, and take a water break. Do not look straight at the sun.

activities.title: Shadow puppet stories
activities.oneLiner: A lamp, your hands, and a wall full of creatures.
activities.whatYouNeed: A torch or lamp, a plain wall, and your two hands. A few cut-out shapes on sticks if you like.
activities.getReady: Dim the room and shine the lamp at a bare wall. Sit so your hands fall between the light and the wall.
activities.howToDoIt: Make a dog, a bird, a snapping crocodile with your hands. Give them voices and act out a little story together on the wall.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their story wherever it goes. Play a character and let them play one back. Ask what happens next rather than steering the plot.
activities.trySaying: "Your bird looks worried. What is it afraid of?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If hand shapes are tricky, cut a simple animal from card and tape it to a stick.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child waggles one hand and watches the shape move.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes the animals big and small by moving hands near and far from the wall, and works out why.
activities.builds: Inventing characters and feeling their way into how each one feels.
activities.whyItWorks: A blank wall and a light are a stage with no script, so the whole story comes from them.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading feelings and telling stories, the glue of getting on with people.
activities.safety: The closer your hand is to the light, the bigger the shadow grows on the wall. Move it toward the wall and it shrinks and sharpens.

activities.title: Draw the shadow, then wait
activities.oneLiner: Where will it be after lunch?
activities.whatYouNeed: Chalk, and something that stays put outside like a pot plant, a toy, or a garden chair. A sunny day.
activities.getReady: In the morning, set the object on a path in the sun. Chalk around its shadow and mark the time with a scribbled sun.
activities.howToDoIt: Come back a few hours later. The shadow has moved and changed length. Draw the new one in chalk beside the first. Talk about what shifted.
activities.howToGuide: Ask them to guess where the shadow will be before you go back out. Let the chalk lines prove or surprise the guess.
activities.trySaying: "Where do you think its shadow will be after lunch?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If they forget in between, set a timer and make the return trip the whole event, snack in hand.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just traces the two shadows and sees they are different.
activities.makeHarder: An older one draws the shadow three times across the day and spots that it swings around and grows toward evening.
activities.builds: Watching a slow change and holding a question in mind across hours.
activities.whyItWorks: The gap between drawings makes the sun's slow move visible, something a single glance would miss.
activities.downTheTrack: Waiting for real evidence before deciding what is true.
activities.safety: Slip, slop, slap for both trips outside, and keep the chalk out of mouths.

activities.title: Guess the shadow
activities.oneLiner: One shape on the sheet. What is making it?
activities.whatYouNeed: A torch, a plain wall or hung sheet, and a basket of everyday objects like a fork, a toy dinosaur, a colander, a hairbrush.
activities.getReady: Dim the room. Sit your child facing the wall and hide the basket behind you where they cannot see you pick.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold one object in the torchlight so only its shadow shows on the wall. They guess what it is from the shape alone, then you reveal it.
activities.howToGuide: Give them time to study the outline. Turn the object slowly so a new angle gives a clue. Ask what part of the shadow gave it away.
activities.trySaying: "Just from the shape, what do you think it is?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If guesses stall, start with objects that have a clear outline like a fork or a cup.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child picks from two objects laid in front of them.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses trickier shapes, or takes a turn making shadows for you to name.
activities.builds: Reading a shape carefully and matching it to what they know.
activities.whyItWorks: With colour and detail stripped away, they have to reason from the outline alone.
activities.downTheTrack: Judging what a thing is from partial clues, without being fooled.
activities.safety: A shadow shows only the outline, not the colour or the inside, which is exactly what makes some easy and some hard.

activities.title: Shadows with your whole body
activities.oneLiner: A dinosaur, a star, a giant on the wall.
activities.whatYouNeed: A big light source. The low sun on a wall outside, or a lamp on a bare indoor wall.
activities.getReady: Find a spot where a whole body shadow falls large and clear. Late afternoon sun on a fence is perfect.
activities.howToDoIt: Use arms, legs, and backs to make shapes. A flapping bird, a spiky dinosaur, a tall tree, two of you joined into one strange creature.
activities.howToGuide: Let them invent the shapes and name them. Join in as a second body when they want something bigger. Ask how they could make themselves look enormous.
activities.trySaying: "Show me the biggest, spikiest monster you can make."
activities.ifNotWorking: If they feel shy, start by copying their shape with your own body so they are not performing alone.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child makes a shadow wave, jump, and grow tall on tiptoes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one combines with you to make one animal with four legs, or freezes a shape for you to guess.
activities.builds: Using their own body as the tool to make something new.
activities.whyItWorks: Their whole self becomes the material, so the making is physical and freeing at once.
activities.downTheTrack: Believing they can make something out of nothing but themselves.
activities.safety: Clear the space of trip hazards before the big moves start, and keep an eye out for hard corners.

activities.title: Make a shadow clock
activities.oneLiner: Tell the time by a stick in the ground.
activities.whatYouNeed: A straight stick, a sunny open patch of dirt or a paved spot, some small stones or chalk.
activities.getReady: Push the stick upright into the ground or stand it in a pot of sand in a sunny place that gets sun all day.
activities.howToDoIt: Each hour or so, mark where the stick's shadow points with a stone or a chalk line and say the time. By the end of the day you have a fan of marks, a real clock made of sun.
activities.howToGuide: Let them place each stone. Ask them to predict which way the next shadow will point. Notice together that the marks fan out in order.
activities.trySaying: "Let's mark it now. Which way will the shadow go next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If a whole day is too long, mark it three times, morning, midday, and afternoon, to still see the swing.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child helps place two stones and sees the shadow moved.
activities.makeHarder: An older one uses the finished marks to guess the time the next sunny day and checks against a real clock.
activities.builds: Linking the sun's steady march to something they built and can read.
activities.whyItWorks: Coming back all day to one growing set of marks shows a real pattern that a quick look never would.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with a long project and seeing how people first read the sky.
activities.safety: Slip, slop, slap for the outdoor visits, and pick a stick with no sharp point for small hands.

themes.bringItTogether: Chase a shadow, trace it, and build a clock from it, and your child starts to see that the sun moves, shapes have secrets, and their own body can make magic on a wall.

themes.title: Seeds and Growing
themes.hook: Plant it, wait, tend it, watch it change.

activities.title: Sprout a bean in a jar
activities.oneLiner: Can you watch a seed wake up?
activities.time: 10 min to set up, then a peek each day
activities.whatYouNeed: A clean jar, a paper towel, a dried bean from the pantry, water.
activities.getReady: Scrunch the paper towel down the inside of the jar. Tuck a bean between the paper and the glass so you can see it.
activities.howToDoIt: Splash a little water in the bottom to keep the towel damp. Put the jar on the windowsill. Look each morning and talk about what has changed.
activities.howToGuide: Do not tell them what will happen. Let them notice the split, the little white root, the first curl of green.
activities.trySaying: "What is different since yesterday?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Nothing moves for a few days at first. That is normal. Keep the towel damp, not soaked.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just checks the water and points at changes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one draws the bean each day and puts the pages in order at the end.
activities.builds: Slowing down enough to spot a tiny change.
activities.whyItWorks: The reward is quiet and slow, so noticing becomes the whole point.
activities.downTheTrack: People who can pay real attention will always see what the fast scrollers miss.
activities.safety: Never eat the bean or any seed, raw beans can make you crook. Wash hands after handling.

activities.title: Plant a pot of something to eat
activities.oneLiner: Can you grow your own snack?
activities.whatYouNeed: An old pot or a bucket with a hole in the bottom, potting mix, a punnet of lettuce or snow pea seedlings from the nursery, water.
activities.getReady: Buy the seedlings. Have the pot and mix ready near a tap.
activities.howToDoIt: Let the child scoop the mix, dig a hole with their fingers, settle each seedling in and firm the soil around it. Water it in. This pot is theirs to look after.
activities.howToGuide: Hands off. Muddy and wonky is fine. They own it.
activities.trySaying: "This one is yours to keep alive."
activities.ifNotWorking: If it wilts in the Aussie sun, move the pot to morning sun and afternoon shade.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child plants one seedling and does the watering.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plants a whole punnet and works out a watering routine.
activities.builds: Doing a real job that a living thing depends on.
activities.whyItWorks: Ownership is powerful, the plant lives or struggles by their hand.
activities.downTheTrack: Knowing you can make real things happen in the real world is the root of confidence.
activities.safety: Wash hands well after soil, some potting mix carries bugs that make you sick. Never eat leaves until an adult says they are ready.

activities.title: Paint with beetroot and other kitchen colours
activities.oneLiner: Can a vegetable be your paintbox?
activities.whatYouNeed: A cooked beetroot, a slice of red cabbage, a spoon of turmeric, paper, a couple of small bowls, old brushes or cotton buds.
activities.getReady: Squeeze the beetroot for pink juice. Soak cabbage in a splash of hot water for purple. Mix turmeric with water for gold. You do the hot bits.
activities.howToDoIt: Sit together and paint a picture using only plant colours. Talk about where each colour comes from.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder out loud alongside them. Let their picture be theirs, paint your own beside it.
activities.trySaying: "Plants made all of these, no shop needed."
activities.ifNotWorking: If colours look weak, use less water. If hands stain, that washes off in a day.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child finger-paints with the beetroot juice.
activities.makeHarder: An older one mixes colours and predicts what they will make.
activities.builds: Making something new from what the garden and kitchen give you.
activities.whyItWorks: Sharing the making, side by side, turns colour into a story you tell together.
activities.downTheTrack: The joy of making things by hand, next to someone you love, is a human thing no machine takes.
activities.safety: These are food colours so they are safe on skin, but painting is not eating, keep it on the paper.

activities.title: Sort the real seeds from the fakes
activities.oneLiner: Which of these could actually grow?
activities.whatYouNeed: A muffin tray or egg carton, a mix of real seeds and lookalikes, think a sunflower seed, a lentil, a bead, a small pebble, a grain of rice, a peppercorn.
activities.getReady: Pop one thing in each cup. Mix the real seeds in with the impostors.
activities.howToDoIt: Ask which ones are seeds that could grow into a plant, and which are not. Talk through the clues. A seed feels a certain way, has a certain shape.
activities.howToGuide: Do not correct too fast. Ask why they think each one is real or fake. Let them defend their guess.
activities.trySaying: "What makes you sure that one is a seed?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Cut a bean open together to show the tiny plant curled inside. Now the difference is real.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts into two piles, hard things and soft things.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plants their picks and checks their guesses over the weeks.
activities.builds: Weighing the evidence before deciding what is true.
activities.whyItWorks: Real and fake sit side by side, so the child has to look closely, not just guess.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling the real from the convincing fake is the skill of the age we are heading into.
activities.safety: Nothing goes in mouths, beads and pebbles choke, and no seed is a snack. Adult stays close.

activities.title: Wait for the radish
activities.oneLiner: Can you be patient for a whole month?
activities.whatYouNeed: A pot or garden patch, radish seeds, a paddle-pop stick, water.
activities.getReady: Radishes are the fastest reward in the veg patch, sprouting in days and ready in about four weeks. Plant a few seeds together.
activities.howToDoIt: Write the date on the stick. Then it is a long game of check, water, wait. Mark how tall the leaves get. Pull one when the shoulder of the radish pokes up.
activities.howToGuide: Do not rush it or pull early to please them. The waiting is the whole lesson.
activities.trySaying: "Slow growing is still growing."
activities.ifNotWorking: If they lose interest, tie the check to something daily like after breakfast.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just does the daily watering.
activities.makeHarder: An older one keeps a tally of days and guesses the harvest date.
activities.builds: Staying with something long after the excitement fades.
activities.whyItWorks: A month is forever to a little kid, so finishing means something.
activities.downTheTrack: The patience to see a slow thing through is rarer, and more valuable, every year.
activities.safety: Wash hands after the soil. Rinse the radish and let an adult say when it is ready to try.

activities.title: Grow a mini herb patch for the family
activities.oneLiner: Can you grow something the whole family cooks with?
activities.whatYouNeed: A shallow tub or a few pots, potting mix, seedlings of basil, parsley or mint, water, labels.
activities.getReady: Pick herbs the family actually eats. Set up near the kitchen door so it gets used.
activities.howToDoIt: The child plants, labels and waters. When a meal needs herbs, they go out and pick them and bring them to the cook.
activities.howToGuide: Let them be the one who decides when it needs water and the one who does the picking. They are the herb keeper.
activities.trySaying: "You grew the parsley for our dinner tonight."
activities.ifNotWorking: Mint takes over, so keep it in its own pot. Basil sulks in cold, so plant it in the warm months.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child looks after one pot of mint, the hardy one.
activities.makeHarder: An older one manages three herbs and works out which likes sun and which likes shade.
activities.builds: Running a real, useful job that the family relies on.
activities.whyItWorks: Feeding the people you love turns a chore into a gift.
activities.downTheTrack: Feeling useful to your people is a quiet kind of confidence that lasts a lifetime.
activities.safety: Wash hands after soil. Only pick and eat the labelled herbs, and let an adult give the first taste.

themes.bringItTogether: Line up the bean jar, the seed sort, and a pinch of picked herbs, and talk about the whole journey, from a sleeping seed to something you tended, waited for, and grew with your own hands.

themes.title: Minibeasts
themes.hook: Ants, snails, spiders and slaters up close.

activities.title: Follow the ant trail
activities.oneLiner: Where is that ant really going?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just your eyes, and maybe a crumb.
activities.getReady: Find a line of ants on a path or wall. Backyards and footpaths are full of them.
activities.howToDoIt: Pick one ant and follow it with your eyes. Where does it go? Does it stop and touch feelers with the others? Watch the trail, not just the one.
activities.howToGuide: Stay low and quiet with them. Do not squash or block the trail. This is watching, not disturbing.
activities.trySaying: "Let's just watch, they are busy working."
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop a tiny crumb near the trail and wait, the ants will find it and the show begins.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just points at ants and counts them.
activities.makeHarder: An older one works out where the trail starts and where it ends.
activities.builds: Holding your focus on one small moving thing in a busy world.
activities.whyItWorks: An ant will not perform on cue, so the child has to slow right down and truly watch.
activities.downTheTrack: Deep focus on the small stuff is how people notice what everyone else races past.
activities.safety: Look, never touch. Some Aussie ants bite or sting, jumper ants and bull ants really hurt, so hands stay back. Wash hands after.

activities.title: Make a slater hotel
activities.oneLiner: Can you build a home for the roly-polies?
activities.whatYouNeed: A shallow container, a damp leaf or two, a bit of bark, a small stone, a spray of water.
activities.getReady: Slaters, the little grey roly-poly ones, live under pots, bark and damp leaves. Lift something gently and you will find them.
activities.howToDoIt: Build a cosy damp corner in the container, then gently scoop a few slaters in with a leaf. Watch how they move, curl and hide. Return them to exactly where you found them within the hour.
activities.howToGuide: Let them do the building and the gentle scooping. Their job is to make the guests comfortable.
activities.trySaying: "How can we make them feel at home?"
activities.ifNotWorking: If the slaters curl up and stop, they are stressed, put them straight back and just watch them in the wild.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child watches one slater on a leaf in their palm, briefly.
activities.makeHarder: An older one designs the hotel with a dark side and a damp side and sees which the slaters pick.
activities.builds: Building a real thing to solve a real creature's needs.
activities.whyItWorks: Slaters are gentle and slow, perfect first guests for small hands.
activities.downTheTrack: Understanding how living things actually work keeps you grounded in the real world, not just the screen.
activities.safety: Slaters are harmless, but wash hands after. Always return minibeasts to where they live. Handle like they are made of glass.

activities.title: Invent a brand new bug
activities.oneLiner: What minibeast has nobody ever seen?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, textas or crayons, and anything odd from the recycling like bottle tops or bits of string, tape.
activities.getReady: Do a bit of real minibeast watching first so their invention has some truth in it.
activities.howToDoIt: Make up a creature that does not exist. How many legs? Does it dig, jump or glow? Give it a name and a home. Draw it or build it.
activities.howToGuide: Do not fix or improve it. Ask what it eats, where it sleeps, and follow their lead.
activities.trySaying: "You are the only person who knows about this one."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start from a real bug and change three things, more legs, a new colour, a funny job.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child adds legs and eyes to a blob you sketch.
activities.makeHarder: An older one writes or tells the story of a day in their bug's life.
activities.builds: Making something brand new that came only from their own head.
activities.whyItWorks: Real bugs give the springboard, then imagination takes over completely.
activities.downTheTrack: The ones who can dream up what does not exist yet will always have something to offer.
activities.safety: There is no wrong answer here, silly is the whole point.

activities.title: Real bug or pretend bug
activities.oneLiner: Is that a leaf, or is it alive?
activities.whatYouNeed: A garden or park, and a keen eye.
activities.getReady: Nature is full of tricks. Stick insects look like twigs, some moths look like bark, a curled leaf can look like a bug.
activities.howToDoIt: Hunt for things that might be alive and might not. For each one, decide is it a real minibeast or is it pretending, or is it just a leaf? Look for the clues, legs, movement, eyes.
activities.howToGuide: Do not answer for them. Ask how they can tell without touching. Watch for a moment to see if it moves.
activities.trySaying: "What clue tells you it is really alive?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start easy with a clearly alive snail and a clearly dead leaf, then build up to the tricky ones.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts finds into alive and not alive.
activities.makeHarder: An older one explains the clue that fooled them and what gave the truth away.
activities.builds: Reading the clues to tell what is real from what only looks it.
activities.whyItWorks: Nature's fakery is a true puzzle, so the child has to look properly and reason.
activities.downTheTrack: Spotting the difference between real and cleverly disguised is a skill worth gold as fakes get better.
activities.safety: Decide with eyes, not fingers. Never touch to check, some things bite or sting. Wash hands after the hunt.

activities.title: Watch a snail cross the path
activities.oneLiner: How far can a snail go before you get bored?
activities.whatYouNeed: A snail, a safe patch of path, patience.
activities.getReady: Snails come out after rain, in the cooler damp months. Find one on the move.
activities.howToDoIt: Set a start point and a finish, say a leaf a hand-span away. Then watch the whole slow journey. Notice the silver trail, the feelers, how it hauls itself along.
activities.howToGuide: Do not hurry the snail or the child. Sitting with the slowness is the lesson. Let them stay till it arrives.
activities.trySaying: "Slow does not mean stopping."
activities.ifNotWorking: If the wait is too long, shorten the finish line, or count the seconds together out loud.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just watches the feelers go in and out.
activities.makeHarder: An older one times the trip or measures the distance with sticks.
activities.builds: Staying with something slow all the way to the end.
activities.whyItWorks: A snail cannot be sped up, so patience is the only way through.
activities.downTheTrack: The patience to see slow things through is a strength that sets people apart.
activities.safety: Snails are gentle, but wash hands well after, they can carry germs. Let it go where you found it.

activities.title: Be a bug carer for a day
activities.oneLiner: Can you keep a little creature safe and let it go?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear container with air holes, a soft leaf, a magnifying glass if you have one.
activities.getReady: Choose a gentle minibeast to visit, a slater, a snail, a caterpillar. Never anything that bites or stings.
activities.howToDoIt: The child is the carer. They gently gather one safe creature, give it a leaf and a damp corner, watch it up close, then, and this is the important part, carry it back and let it go exactly where it came from.
activities.howToGuide: Let them make the calls, gentle hands, when to let go. You are just the safety net.
activities.trySaying: "We look after it, then we set it free."
activities.ifNotWorking: If they want to keep it, talk about its family and home waiting for it. Letting go is part of caring.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just holds the leaf and watches, you do the gathering.
activities.makeHarder: An older one finds out what their creature eats and where it likes to live.
activities.builds: Caring for something small and putting its needs first.
activities.whyItWorks: Being trusted to be gentle, then to let go, is a real act of kindness.
activities.downTheTrack: Caring about other living things, and knowing when to let go, is the heart of being a good human.
activities.safety: Only ever handle safe minibeasts, no ants, bees, spiders or centipedes, they bite and sting. Gentle hands, short visit, always release. Wash hands after.

themes.bringItTogether: Sit down after and talk it over, which minibeast surprised you, which was the gentlest, and remember the golden rule, we look closely, we are kind, and we always put them back where they belong.

themes.title: The Beach
themes.hook: Sand, shells, tide lines and rock pools. A whole world at the water's edge, all of it free.

activities.title: Watch a rock pool wake up
activities.oneLiner: What lives in this little puddle of sea?
activities.whatYouNeed: Bare eyes, a bit of patience, maybe a hat.
activities.getReady: Find a rock pool at low tide and sit down beside it.
activities.howToDoIt: Go still and watch one pool. Wait for it to show you a crab, a tiny fish, a snail on the move.
activities.howToGuide: Don't point everything out. Let the waiting do the work and let them spot the first mover.
activities.trySaying: "Let's stay still and see what comes out."
activities.ifNotWorking: Pick a smaller pool with clearer water so there is less to scan.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child watches for just one thing that moves.
activities.makeHarder: An older one counts how many different creatures live in one pool.
activities.builds: Holding still long enough for a shy world to appear.
activities.whyItWorks: A rock pool only rewards the child who waits and looks closely.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing what others rush past will matter when machines handle the obvious.
activities.safety: Stay at the water's edge with an adult in reach, mind the rips, and leave every creature exactly where it lives. Watch for slippery rocks.

activities.title: Sort the tide line treasure
activities.oneLiner: Which of these came from something alive?
activities.whatYouNeed: A handful of finds from the sand, an old ice-cream tub.
activities.getReady: Walk the tide line and collect empty shells, bits of coral, dry seaweed, smooth glass, driftwood.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort the pile into groups. Once alive or never alive. Rough or smooth. Yours to keep or better left.
activities.howToGuide: Ask before you correct. Let them explain why a thing goes where it goes.
activities.trySaying: "How did you decide that one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Sort by just one rule, like smooth things in one pile.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts by colour.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses what each shell's animal looked like.
activities.builds: Making a careful call about what is what.
activities.whyItWorks: Sorting forces a real judgement, not a guess.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling real from lookalike is the skill of a good decider.
activities.safety: Only empty shells, and check no creature is home. Never touch bluebottles or jellyfish, they sting even washed up and dead. Watch for broken shells and glass.

activities.title: Build a castle the tide can't beat
activities.oneLiner: Can you keep the sea out of your castle?
activities.whatYouNeed: Hands, a bucket or old container, wet sand.
activities.getReady: Set up above the water on damp sand, near enough to watch the tide creep in.
activities.howToDoIt: Build a castle with a wall and a moat. Then defend it as the water rises. Patch, pile, and dig faster.
activities.howToGuide: When a wall caves, resist fixing it. Hand them more sand and let them try again.
activities.trySaying: "The water's coming. What will you do?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Move higher up the beach so the tide gives you more time.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just fills and tips the bucket.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds channels to send the water somewhere else.
activities.builds: Doing a real job with your own two hands against a real clock.
activities.whyItWorks: The tide is honest feedback that never argues.
activities.downTheTrack: Backyard grit and hands-on problem solving hold their value whatever the tools change.
activities.safety: Never leave a child near water, an adult always within reach. Slip, slop, slap. Mind hot dry sand on bare feet.

activities.title: Beachcomb a story home
activities.oneLiner: What tale does this old thing want to tell?
activities.whatYouNeed: One special find, and each other.
activities.getReady: Let each person pick one thing from the sand that catches their eye.
activities.howToDoIt: Take turns making up where it came from. A pipi that crossed an ocean, a stick that was once a pirate mast. Build the story together.
activities.howToGuide: Add one silly line, then hand the story straight back to them.
activities.trySaying: "And then what happened to it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start the story yourself and pause so they finish the sentence.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just names who the thing belongs to.
activities.makeHarder: An older one gives it a beginning, middle and end.
activities.builds: Spinning a whole world out of one small object.
activities.whyItWorks: A bare object leaves all the good bits for the child to invent.
activities.downTheTrack: Making something new from almost nothing is the part no machine hands you.
activities.safety: A washed-up cuttlebone is the inner shell of a cuttlefish, and parrots and budgies love a nibble of one.

activities.title: Draw the whole sea in the sand
activities.oneLiner: How big can you make your masterpiece?
activities.whatYouNeed: A stick, a wide stretch of flat wet sand.
activities.getReady: Find smooth sand near the water's edge where the last wave has flattened it.
activities.howToDoIt: Draw giant pictures with a stick. A whale longer than you are tall, a family portrait in the sand, waves swallowing it all.
activities.howToGuide: Draw your own thing beside theirs, don't fix theirs. Let the sea rub it out and start fresh.
activities.trySaying: "Show me the biggest one you can."
activities.ifNotWorking: Draw a simple shape and ask them to add one thing to it.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child drags the stick to make any marks at all.
activities.makeHarder: An older one draws a scene with three things in it.
activities.builds: Making bold marks and owning the whole big picture.
activities.whyItWorks: Sand you can wipe clean makes trying easy and mistakes free.
activities.downTheTrack: The nerve to make something and start over feeds a lifetime of making.
activities.safety: Stay at the water's edge with an adult in reach, and watch for broken shells and glass in the sand.

activities.title: Listen for the sea's quiet
activities.oneLiner: Close your eyes. How many sounds can you hear?
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing but your ears.
activities.getReady: Sit together on dry sand a little back from the water.
activities.howToDoIt: Close your eyes and stay quiet. Count the sounds. Waves, gulls, wind, a distant dog, each other breathing.
activities.howToGuide: Sit in the quiet with them. Don't fill the gaps with talk.
activities.trySaying: "What can you hear that I might have missed?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just the waves, then add one more sound at a time.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child listens for ten slow seconds.
activities.makeHarder: An older one points in the direction each sound comes from.
activities.builds: Being comfortable in the quiet and staying with it.
activities.whyItWorks: With eyes shut, the only thing to do is keep paying attention.
activities.downTheTrack: Sitting still with your own thoughts is getting rare, and rarer things get precious.
activities.safety: Silver gulls are the cheeky ones after your chips, and they are the only gull most of us ever meet up close.

themes.bringItTogether: Six ways to slow down at the water's edge, where the sea does half the teaching and you just have to be there beside them.

themes.title: Rocks and Dirt
themes.hook: Dig, sort, stack, and get properly grubby. The backyard is a building site, a laboratory and an art studio all at once.

activities.title: Dig a hole to nowhere
activities.oneLiner: How deep can you get before smoko?
activities.whatYouNeed: An old spoon or trowel, a patch of dirt you're allowed to dig, a bucket of water.
activities.getReady: Pick a corner of the garden and give them the green light to dig it up.
activities.howToDoIt: Dig a proper hole. Notice how the dirt changes as you go down, dry on top, cool and dark below. Add water and feel it turn to claggy mud.
activities.howToGuide: Let them set the goal and hit the hard bits on their own. Your job is to keep handing over the bucket.
activities.trySaying: "You keep going. I reckon you can get deeper."
activities.ifNotWorking: Loosen the top layer first so their spoon can bite.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child fills and empties the bucket.
activities.makeHarder: An older one digs to find where the dirt changes colour.
activities.builds: Sticking at a slow job because you chose it yourself.
activities.whyItWorks: Dirt gives way slowly, so the reward only comes to the one who keeps digging.
activities.downTheTrack: The habit of pushing through a boring middle bit is worth more than any shortcut.
activities.safety: Never put rocks or dirt in mouths, it can choke or carry germs. Check for sharp rocks and glass, and wash hands well after.

activities.title: Sort the rock collection
activities.oneLiner: Can you find two rocks exactly the same?
activities.whatYouNeed: A pile of rocks and pebbles, an egg carton or muffin tray.
activities.getReady: Gather a mixed handful of rocks from the garden or driveway.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort them into the tray. By size, by colour, by rough and smooth, by heavy and light. Then look for two that truly match.
activities.howToGuide: Ask how they sorted rather than telling them how. Let a wrong-looking group stand if they can explain it.
activities.trySaying: "What makes these two go together?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Give them just three rocks and one rule.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child puts big in one cup, small in another.
activities.makeHarder: An older one sorts by two rules at once, like small and smooth.
activities.builds: Spotting the fine difference between two things that look alike.
activities.whyItWorks: No two rocks are the same, so every sort is a real decision.
activities.downTheTrack: Careful sorting is judgement in training, and judgement is what stays human.
activities.safety: Never put rocks in mouths, and wash hands after. Check the pile for sharp edges and broken glass first.

activities.title: Build a tower that won't topple
activities.oneLiner: How high before it all comes down?
activities.whatYouNeed: A stack of flat-ish rocks and pebbles.
activities.getReady: Hunt for the flattest stones you can find and pile them nearby.
activities.howToDoIt: Balance rock on rock to build the tallest tower you can. When it falls, and it will, start again and go higher.
activities.howToGuide: Bite your tongue when it wobbles. Let them feel where the balance is with their own hands.
activities.trySaying: "It fell. What will you try this time?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with the biggest flattest rock as a base.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child stacks just two or three.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds on a wobbly or sloped surface.
activities.builds: Trying again calmly after the whole thing tumbles.
activities.whyItWorks: Balance can't be rushed, so patience is the only way up.
activities.downTheTrack: Staying steady when things collapse is a strength no clever tool can hand you.
activities.safety: Check under rocks for spiders before hands go in, mind sharp edges, and keep the tower low enough that a falling rock can't land on toes.

activities.title: Cook up a mud kitchen feast
activities.oneLiner: What's on the menu at your restaurant today?
activities.whatYouNeed: Old pots, spoons, cups, dirt, water, leaves and petals for garnish.
activities.getReady: Set out the tin gear near a dirt patch and a bucket of water.
activities.howToDoIt: Run a restaurant. Mix mud pies, chocolate soup and gum-leaf salad. Take each other's orders and serve up the specials.
activities.howToGuide: Be the customer, not the chef. Order things and let them decide how to make them.
activities.trySaying: "I'll have your special. What's in it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Order one simple thing, a mud biscuit, to get the game rolling.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just stirs and pours.
activities.makeHarder: An older one names dishes and remembers the whole order.
activities.builds: Running the whole pretend world and inviting you into it.
activities.whyItWorks: An open kitchen means every dish is theirs to invent.
activities.downTheTrack: Pretending and inventing on the spot is the root of every new idea.
activities.safety: Never put dirt or leaves in mouths, some Aussie plants like oleander are toxic. Wash hands well after cooking.

activities.title: Peek under a rock
activities.oneLiner: Who's hiding in the cool and the dark?
activities.whatYouNeed: A stick, curious eyes, a garden with a few loose rocks or logs.
activities.getReady: Find a rock or log that's been sitting a while in a damp spot.
activities.howToDoIt: Tip it gently and look at the little world underneath. Slaters, worms, ants, maybe a beetle. Watch, then put the roof back on their home.
activities.howToGuide: Let them lift and look. Wonder out loud about who lives there rather than naming everything.
activities.trySaying: "Where do you reckon they were all heading?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Choose a spot near the tap where the ground stays damp and busy.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child watches one slater roll into a ball.
activities.makeHarder: An older one counts the different minibeasts and gently sets the rock back exactly as it was.
activities.builds: Wondering about a hidden world and caring for the creatures in it.
activities.whyItWorks: Under every rock is a real question with a live answer.
activities.downTheTrack: Wanting to know what's underneath is the engine behind every discovery.
activities.safety: Always check under a rock with a stick first, redbacks and other spiders shelter there. Never reach a bare hand into a dark gap, and wash hands after.

activities.title: Paint with dirt and stone
activities.oneLiner: Which rock draws, and which one won't?
activities.whatYouNeed: A few rocks of different colours, a splash of water, an old plate, a bit of paper or a paved path.
activities.getReady: Collect some soft crumbly rocks, some hard ones, and a little red or yellow dirt.
activities.howToDoIt: Test which rocks leave a mark and which won't. Mix dirt with water to make a paint. Make a picture together on paper or the path.
activities.howToGuide: Let them test and decide which rock is the good one. Paint alongside them without touching theirs.
activities.trySaying: "Try that one. Does it leave a colour?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with soft chalky sandstone, which marks easily.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child scribbles with one marking rock.
activities.makeHarder: An older one sorts the rocks into draws and won't-draw before painting.
activities.builds: Testing what works, then making something with it.
activities.whyItWorks: Every rock tests a small guess, so making becomes deciding too.
activities.downTheTrack: Judging what's fit for the job, then building with it, is craft that lasts.
activities.safety: Ochre is coloured earth, and First Nations peoples have painted with it for tens of thousands of years. Rinse the path clean after with water.

themes.bringItTogether: Six ways to get grubby in the backyard, where a patch of dirt turns into a dig site, a science bench and a paint set, and the mess washes right off.

themes.title: Trees and leaves
themes.hook: Bark to climb, leaves to sort and print. The backyard gum becomes a whole afternoon.

activities.title: Bark rubbings
activities.oneLiner: What is hiding under the paper?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, a few peeled crayons, a tree with interesting bark.
activities.getReady: Peel the paper off two or three crayons before you head out.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold the paper flat on the bark. Rub the side of the crayon over it and watch the pattern rise up.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose the bark they want to copy. Hold the paper steady only if they ask.
activities.trySaying: "What can you feel under the paper?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Try a smoother gum trunk and press harder with the crayon on its side.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child rubs a fallen piece of bark held flat on the ground.
activities.makeHarder: An older one collects three barks and labels which tree each came from.
activities.builds: Noticing tiny detail your eyes would otherwise skate straight over.
activities.whyItWorks: The pattern only appears when the hand stays slow and even.
activities.downTheTrack: Close looking, the quiet habit under reading and drawing.
activities.safety: Check the bark for ants and spiders before you press on it, and wash hands after. Never put bark or leaves in mouths.

activities.title: Climb a low branch
activities.oneLiner: How high is too high today?
activities.whatYouNeed: A sturdy low tree, closed shoes, an adult within arm's reach.
activities.getReady: Pick a tree with a thick branch near the ground. Check the ground under it is clear.
activities.howToDoIt: Let them find hand holds and foot holds and climb only as high as your arms can reach.
activities.howToGuide: Stand close. Ask before you lift. Let them work out where each foot goes.
activities.trySaying: "Test that branch. Does it hold?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with one foot up and both hands on the trunk. That counts as a climb.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child steps onto a low fork and back down.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plans a route up and back before they start.
activities.builds: Judging their own body against a real risk.
activities.whyItWorks: A branch gives honest feedback a parent's warning cannot.
activities.downTheTrack: Sizing up a challenge and backing their own judgement.
activities.safety: Low and supervised only. Check the branch takes weight before they trust it. Watch for ants, spiders and loose bark, and wash hands after. Never eat anything off the tree.

activities.title: Sort the leaf pile
activities.oneLiner: How many ways can these leaves be grouped?
activities.whatYouNeed: A handful of fallen leaves in different shapes and sizes.
activities.getReady: Gather a mixed pile of dry fallen leaves together.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort them into groups. Big and small, then smooth and toothy, then by colour. Change the rule and sort again.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what makes two leaves belong together. Follow their rule even if it seems odd.
activities.trySaying: "Why does that one go with those?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just two piles, big and little.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child matches two leaves that look the same.
activities.makeHarder: An older one sorts by a hidden rule and you guess what it is.
activities.builds: Telling one thing from another and saying why.
activities.whyItWorks: The same pile can be split a dozen true ways.
activities.downTheTrack: Sorting and classifying, the root of early science and maths.
activities.safety: Pick up fallen leaves only, and wash hands after. Never taste them, as many Australian leaves are toxic.

activities.title: Print with leaves and gumnuts
activities.oneLiner: What mark does a gum leaf leave behind?
activities.whatYouNeed: Fallen leaves and gumnuts, a little paint, paper, an old plate.
activities.getReady: Spread a thin layer of paint on the plate. Lay out the paper.
activities.howToDoIt: Press a leaf into the paint, then onto the paper. Look at the veins that print. Build a pattern across the page together.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose which leaf and where it goes. Resist tidying their page.
activities.trySaying: "Let's see what the back of the leaf prints."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a chunkier leaf that holds more paint, and press it under a second sheet.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child stamps one leaf over and over.
activities.makeHarder: An older one prints a whole tree, trunk to leaves.
activities.builds: Turning a real object into a print you design.
activities.whyItWorks: Every leaf hides a vein map you only see once it prints.
activities.downTheTrack: Seeing structure in nature, and making art from what is close by.
activities.safety: Use fallen leaves only, and wash hands well after painting. Keep leaves and gumnuts out of mouths.

activities.title: Meet a tree
activities.oneLiner: Can you find your tree again with your eyes shut?
activities.whatYouNeed: A small group of trees in a park or yard, a blindfold or just closed eyes.
activities.getReady: Choose an area with a few trees close together.
activities.howToDoIt: Lead them gently to one tree. They feel the bark, the roots, the low branches. Lead them back, then they open their eyes and find that tree again.
activities.howToGuide: Guide their hands to notice, then let them lead the search back.
activities.trySaying: "What will help you know this tree again?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Keep eyes open the first time and just study one tree closely.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child hugs and feels one tree, no blindfold.
activities.makeHarder: An older one describes their tree to you so you can find it.
activities.builds: Knowing a living thing by touch, not just sight.
activities.whyItWorks: With eyes shut the hands and the memory have to do the work.
activities.downTheTrack: Paying warm attention to the living world, and to each other.
activities.safety: Walk slowly with them while blindfolded and clear trip hazards first. Check bark for ants and spiders, and wash hands after.

activities.title: Build with fallen sticks
activities.oneLiner: Can you build something that stands on its own?
activities.whatYouNeed: Fallen sticks of different lengths, an open patch of ground.
activities.getReady: Collect a pile of dry fallen sticks together.
activities.howToDoIt: Build something that stands. A tower, a teepee, a bridge. When it falls, work out why and fix it.
activities.howToGuide: Let it fall. Ask what to change before you offer an idea.
activities.trySaying: "Which stick should go at the bottom?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Lean a few sticks together into a simple teepee shape first.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child lays sticks longest to shortest in a row.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds to a set height, or a bridge two hands wide.
activities.builds: Choosing the right piece for the job and testing if it holds.
activities.whyItWorks: A leaning tower shows the problem the moment it topples.
activities.downTheTrack: Planning, testing and rebuilding, the maker's loop.
activities.safety: Blunt sticks only, carried pointing down. Check for ants and spiders, and wash hands after. Nothing goes near mouths or eyes.

themes.bringItTogether: One tree gives you a climb, a texture, a sort, a print and a quiet minute of listening. Come back to the same gum next week and see what has changed.

themes.title: Wind
themes.hook: You can't see it, but you can feel it, catch it, race it and put it to work. A windy day is a full afternoon.

activities.title: Read the wind
activities.oneLiner: Which way is the wind going today?
activities.whatYouNeed: A ribbon or a strip of a plastic bag tied to a stick, or just wet fingers.
activities.getReady: Tie a light ribbon to the end of a stick.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold the ribbon up and watch which way it streams. Turn around. Find where the wind comes from and where it goes.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide the direction. Ask how they can tell.
activities.trySaying: "Which way is it pushing the ribbon?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Wet a finger and hold it up. The cool side faces the wind.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just watches the ribbon dance.
activities.makeHarder: An older one checks the wind in three spots to see if it changes.
activities.builds: Reading something you can feel but cannot see.
activities.whyItWorks: The ribbon makes an invisible force show itself.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing the weather and how the world moves.
activities.safety: Sun hat and shade breaks. If dust is blowing, keep it out of eyes and head inside.

activities.title: Make a windsock
activities.oneLiner: Can you catch the wind in a paper tube?
activities.whatYouNeed: A sheet of paper or a paper bag, tape, string, streamers of scrap paper.
activities.getReady: Roll the paper into a tube and tape it. Tape paper streamers around one end.
activities.howToDoIt: Tie string to the open end and hold it up. Watch the wind fill it and the streamers fly. Try it in a gusty spot and a calm one.
activities.howToGuide: Let them build it and choose where to test it.
activities.trySaying: "Where's the windiest spot to try it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Add lighter streamers and hold it higher.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child holds a single streamer up to the wind.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds a tail and makes it spin.
activities.builds: Making a thing that turns wind into movement you can see.
activities.whyItWorks: A loose sock catches gusts a flat page would miss.
activities.downTheTrack: Building to test an idea, then improving it.
activities.safety: Hat and sun cover. Keep the string short and stay well away from roads and powerlines.

activities.title: Race the wind
activities.oneLiner: Can you run faster than a leaf on the breeze?
activities.whatYouNeed: Light things that blow, like leaves, a feather, a scrap of paper. An open grassy space.
activities.getReady: Find an open patch of grass away from roads.
activities.howToDoIt: Drop a leaf and chase it as the wind carries it. Race a friend or a parent. Try to reach it before it lands.
activities.howToGuide: Let them pick what to race and set the finish line.
activities.trySaying: "Ready? Let's see who beats the leaf."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a lighter thing like a feather that drifts slower and further.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child chases a scarf you drag along the ground.
activities.makeHarder: An older one predicts where it will land and waits there.
activities.builds: Reading where the wind will take a thing and moving to meet it.
activities.whyItWorks: Chasing turns a windy day into a game with a real rival.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with a game that keeps changing, and sharing it.
activities.safety: Open grass only, well away from roads, fences and water. Keep eyes up so no one collides.

activities.title: Make a pinwheel
activities.oneLiner: Can you build something the wind will spin?
activities.whatYouNeed: A square of paper, a pin or a split pin, a stick or pencil, scissors.
activities.getReady: Cut from each corner towards the middle, not all the way. Fold every second point in and pin them to the stick.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold it up to the wind or blow on it. Watch it spin. Try holding it higher, or running with it, to make it turn faster.
activities.howToGuide: Let them fold and test. Let them work out what makes it spin faster.
activities.trySaying: "What makes it go faster?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Loosen the pin so the paper spins free, and try a gust or a good blow.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child blows on a pinwheel you made.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes two sizes and works out which spins easier.
activities.builds: Seeing wind do real work when it turns the blades.
activities.whyItWorks: The folds catch the air and push the wheel around.
activities.downTheTrack: A first feel for how machines turn a push into motion.
activities.safety: An adult handles the pin and pushes it in. Cap the sharp end against the stick so no point sticks out.

activities.title: Listen to the wind
activities.oneLiner: What sounds does the wind make things do?
activities.whatYouNeed: Old keys, spoons or bottle caps and some string, or just your ears.
activities.getReady: Tie a few metal odds and ends to a stick so they nearly touch. Hang it where the breeze reaches.
activities.howToDoIt: Sit quietly and listen. What clinks, what rustles, what taps. Name each sound the wind makes together.
activities.howToGuide: Stay quiet with them. Let the listening last a little longer than feels comfortable.
activities.trySaying: "Shh. What can you hear the wind doing?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Close eyes and listen for just one sound at a time.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child listens to leaves rustling, no chimes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one closes their eyes and counts how many sounds they hear.
activities.builds: Holding still and letting the ears lead.
activities.whyItWorks: Wind is silent until it has something to play.
activities.downTheTrack: Quiet focus, and delight in small everyday things.
activities.safety: Keep small metal bits and string well out of reach when not hung up, and hang the chime where little ones cannot pull it down.

activities.title: Will it fly?
activities.oneLiner: Which things will the wind carry, and which won't?
activities.whatYouNeed: A small basket of safe things, like a leaf, a feather, a pebble, a gumnut, a scrap of paper.
activities.getReady: Gather a few light and heavy things into a basket. Head somewhere breezy.
activities.howToDoIt: Guess which will blow away and which will drop. Hold each one up and let go. Sort them into flies and falls.
activities.howToGuide: Let them guess first, then test. Ask why the pebble stayed put.
activities.trySaying: "Will this one fly or fall? What do you think?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with the two clearest, a feather and a pebble.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just drops things and watches.
activities.makeHarder: An older one lines things up from lightest to heaviest first.
activities.builds: Guessing an outcome, then checking it against what happens.
activities.whyItWorks: Light things lose to the wind and heavy things win, every time.
activities.downTheTrack: Predicting and testing, the heart of how science starts.
activities.safety: Choose things too big to swallow, and keep pebbles and gumnuts out of mouths. Test away from roads.

themes.bringItTogether: The wind you read in the first minute is the same wind that spins the pinwheel and carries the feather. Point it out again next windy day and watch them notice sooner.

themes.title: Rain and Puddles
themes.hook: Grey skies are an invitation. When the rain comes, pull on the gumboots and go and meet it together.

activities.title: Puddle jump champions
activities.oneLiner: How big a splash can two feet make?
activities.whatYouNeed: Gumboots, a raincoat, a safe flat puddle away from the road.
activities.getReady: Find a puddle on grass, a path or the backyard, well clear of gutters, drains and traffic.
activities.howToDoIt: Take turns jumping in. Try a tiny tiptoe splash, then the biggest bomb you can. Notice who makes the water fly highest.
activities.howToGuide: Let them find their own jumping style. Cheer the effort, not just the big splashes.
activities.trySaying: "Show me your biggest splash yet."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start by stomping one boot, then two, then a small hop.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child stamps at the edge and watches the ripples.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses which puddle will splash highest and tests it.
activities.builds: Trusting your own body to try something bold and a bit wild.
activities.whyItWorks: A puddle gives instant feedback, so every jump teaches something.
activities.downTheTrack: The gutsy kid who backs their own go grows into someone who acts, not just watches.
activities.safety: Never drink puddle water. Wet paths and tiles are slippery, so stay on grass or rough ground. Keep well back from roads, gutters and stormwater drains. Come inside at the first thunder or lightning. Warm dry clothes straight after.

activities.title: Bark boat regatta
activities.oneLiner: Which little boat will win the race?
activities.whatYouNeed: Bits of bark, gum leaves, twigs, a bottle top or two, a puddle or trickle of runoff.
activities.getReady: Collect a small pile of floaty bits from under the gum trees after the rain.
activities.howToDoIt: Launch different boats and watch. Which floats, which sinks, which sails the furthest? Build a favourite and race it.
activities.howToGuide: Ask them to guess before each launch, then look together at what really happened.
activities.trySaying: "Which one do you reckon will float?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop a leaf in first, so they see a clear win before testing trickier bits.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just drops things in and watches them bob.
activities.makeHarder: An older one loads a leaf with pebbles to find the tipping point.
activities.builds: Testing a hunch against what the water actually does.
activities.whyItWorks: Guessing then checking is real thinking, and being wrong is half the fun.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling a good guess from a proven fact is the skill that keeps you clear-headed when machines sound sure.
activities.safety: Bark, gum leaves and gumnuts float well because they trap air. A wet rock never will.

activities.title: Follow the flow
activities.oneLiner: Where does all this water go?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just your eyes, and gumboots for wandering.
activities.getReady: Wait for a light steady rain or the minutes just after it eases.
activities.howToDoIt: Pick a trickle of water and follow it. Watch it find the low spots, pool, then slide on. Where does it end up?
activities.howToGuide: Go slow and quiet. Let them lead the way and spot the next bit of the path.
activities.trySaying: "Let's follow it and see where it wants to go."
activities.ifNotWorking: Trickle a cup of water down a slope to make a stream to chase.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child watches one puddle fill and points where it spills.
activities.makeHarder: An older one predicts the route before you walk it.
activities.builds: Holding your gaze on one quiet thing and really watching it.
activities.whyItWorks: Water always takes the low road, so there is a real pattern to notice.
activities.downTheTrack: Deep noticing is getting rare and precious, and it is where the best questions come from.
activities.safety: Follow water on paths and grass only. Never follow it toward a road, gutter, drain or creek. Come inside in thunder and lightning, and change into dry clothes after.

activities.title: Rain on the roof orchestra
