activities.oneLiner: What song is the rain playing today?
activities.whatYouNeed: A few upturned pots, an ice cream container, a metal tin, a wooden spoon.
activities.getReady: Set your containers out under the drips off the veranda or eave, in a safe dry spot to stand.
activities.howToDoIt: Listen first to the rain hitting different surfaces. Then set up your own drips and play along. Loud tin, soft plastic, deep pot.
activities.howToGuide: Sit close and listen together before you make a sound. Match their rhythm, do not lead it.
activities.trySaying: "Shhh, what can you hear right now?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Tap the containers yourself with a finger to show the different notes.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child bangs one pot and grins.
activities.makeHarder: An older one copies a rhythm you tap, then makes one for you.
activities.builds: Quiet, shared attention and the joy of making sound side by side.
activities.whyItWorks: Listening close, then answering, is the heart of every good conversation.
activities.downTheTrack: Being fully present with another person is the human thing no screen can hand back to you.
activities.safety: Rain sounds different on tin, tile and leaves because each surface shakes the air its own way.

activities.title: Catch the rain
activities.oneLiner: How much rain fell while we waited?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clean straight-sided jar or cup, a texta or sticky tape.
activities.getReady: Set the jar out in the open, away from the eaves, at the start of a shower.
activities.howToDoIt: Leave it to fill. Come back later and mark the water line. Was it more or less than you guessed? Try again next rain.
activities.howToGuide: Let the waiting be the point. Guess together, then trust the jar to settle the answer.
activities.trySaying: "Do you think it will reach your line?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Half-fill the jar first so the change is easier to spot.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just checks if it is wetter or fuller than before.
activities.makeHarder: An older one marks the level each hour and compares.
activities.builds: Patience for a slow result, and reading it honestly.
activities.whyItWorks: The jar does not lie, so guesses meet real evidence.
activities.downTheTrack: Waiting well and judging by what actually happened beats jumping to the first easy answer.
activities.safety: A rain gauge only reads true in the open, because eaves and trees steal or dump extra water.

activities.title: Worm rescue
activities.oneLiner: Who needs a hand back to the garden?
activities.whatYouNeed: A leaf or small stick to scoop, gentle hands.
activities.getReady: Head out to a path or driveway just after rain, when worms and snails come up.
activities.howToDoIt: Look for worms and snails stranded on hard ground. Gently lift each one on a leaf and pop it back onto soil or into the garden bed.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their pace and care. Let them decide how to lift each little one safely.
activities.trySaying: "How can we help this one get home?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Rescue the first one yourself so they see how gentle to be.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child points them out for you to move.
activities.makeHarder: An older one works out why the worms came up and where the safest soil is.
activities.builds: Small brave kindness and the feeling of being someone who helps.
activities.whyItWorks: Caring for a tiny creature makes a big feeling fit in little hands.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing who needs help and choosing to act is a warmth that stays valuable no matter what changes.
activities.safety: Wash hands well after touching worms, snails and wet ground. Stay clear of roads and drains. Do not handle slugs or snail bait, and come inside in thunder and lightning.

themes.bringItTogether: Over a week of showers, jump the puddles, race the boats, follow the flow, play the rain, catch it in a jar and rescue the worms. Same rain, six ways to meet it, and a child who learns weather is something to step into, not hide from.

themes.title: The Kitchen
themes.hook: The kitchen is a little science lab you already own. Mix, measure, taste, and watch ordinary things turn into something new, side by side.

activities.title: Banana smash on toast
activities.oneLiner: Can you turn a lumpy banana into breakfast?
activities.whatYouNeed: A ripe banana, a bowl, a fork, toast, a plate.
activities.getReady: You make the toast and let it cool a little. Set out the banana and bowl.
activities.howToDoIt: The child peels and mashes the banana with the fork until smooth, then spreads it on the cool toast and sprinkles a little cinnamon.
activities.howToGuide: Let them wrestle the lumps. Do not grab the fork when it gets slow.
activities.trySaying: "Keep going, you're squashing the last lumps."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with a very ripe banana that mashes with barely any push.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child mashes while you steady the bowl.
activities.makeHarder: An older one mashes, spreads it right to the edges and cuts triangles with a butter knife.
activities.builds: Real hands-on know-how and the pride of making your own food.
activities.whyItWorks: A fork and a banana give a small child a job they can truly finish.
activities.downTheTrack: Practical, I-can-do-this competence is a steady kind of confidence a screen never teaches.
activities.safety: The toaster, stove and hot water are adult jobs. Check for allergies first. Only a soft butter knife for little hands, and watch for choking with any firm bits.

activities.title: The measuring team
activities.oneLiner: Can you fill the cup right to the line?
activities.whatYouNeed: A dry measuring cup, oats or flour, a mixing bowl, a spoon.
activities.getReady: Set out the cup and a bowl of oats where nothing can spill far.
activities.howToDoIt: Scoop and pour to fill the cup exactly to the top, no more, no less. Level it with a finger. Tip it in the bowl and count how many cups make the mix.
activities.howToGuide: Let them judge full by eye. Ask if that scoop looks like too much or not enough.
activities.trySaying: "Is that over the line or under?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a smaller cup and a bigger scoop so filling it is quick and clear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just tips a scoop in and stirs.
activities.makeHarder: An older one measures two cups and works out how many for a double batch.
activities.builds: Careful eyes and the judgement of just right, not too much.
activities.whyItWorks: A line on a cup turns a vague idea into something you can check.
activities.downTheTrack: Weighing up enough, too much and not quite is judgement, and judgement is what steers every good decision.
activities.safety: Baking is one of the few kinds of cooking where measuring carefully really does change the result.

activities.title: The blindfold taste test
activities.oneLiner: Can your tongue guess what your eyes can't see?
activities.whatYouNeed: Small bits of safe soft food, a tea towel for a blindfold.
activities.getReady: You slice a few Aussie favourites like banana, soft pear, cucumber and a little Vegemite on bread.
activities.howToDoIt: Blindfold the taster. Pop one food in and let them guess. Is it sweet, salty, sour? What is it? Swap turns.
activities.howToGuide: Slow them down to taste properly before guessing. Ask what their tongue notices first.
activities.trySaying: "Taste it slowly, then tell me what you know."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with strong easy flavours like Vegemite or a slice of orange.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child keeps eyes open and just names the taste.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses the food and whether it is sweet, salty or sour.
activities.builds: Paying close attention to the senses and naming what is real.
activities.whyItWorks: Taking sight away makes the other senses wake right up.
activities.downTheTrack: Trusting your own careful read of something, not just the label on it, keeps you sharp.
activities.safety: Check for allergies before you begin. Cut everything soft and small, sit down to eat, and watch closely for choking. No nuts or hard raw veg for little ones.

activities.title: Shake it into butter
activities.oneLiner: Can you turn cream into something new by shaking?
activities.whatYouNeed: Thickened cream, a clean jar with a tight lid, a pinch of salt.
activities.getReady: Half-fill the jar with cream and screw the lid on hard yourself.
activities.howToDoIt: Shake and shake. It goes to whipped, then thick, then suddenly a yellow lump of butter splits from the liquid. Spread the butter on bread.
activities.howToGuide: Let the mystery build. Do not tell them what is coming, let them feel it change.
activities.trySaying: "Keep shaking, something's about to happen."
activities.ifNotWorking: Take turns when arms get tired, and check that the cream is thickened, not light.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child shakes with two hands while you cheer the count.
activities.makeHarder: An older one watches for each stage and names them in order.
activities.builds: Wonder at a plain thing becoming a new thing in your own hands.
activities.whyItWorks: A change you cause yourself feels like magic and sticks in the memory.
activities.downTheTrack: Curiosity about how and why things work is the engine behind every new idea.
activities.safety: Shaking bumps the fat in cream together until it clumps into butter and leaves buttermilk behind. It is a real change you can eat.

activities.title: Pikelets for someone we love
activities.oneLiner: Who could we make a little stack for?
activities.whatYouNeed: Self-raising flour, milk, an egg, a bowl, a whisk, a pan (adult).
activities.getReady: Choose together who the pikelets are for. Set out the bowl and ingredients.
activities.howToDoIt: The child cracks the egg, pours the milk, whisks the batter and adds a few sultanas. You cook them on the pan. Together you plate a little stack for someone special.
activities.howToGuide: Let them own the mixing and the mess. Talk about who will love these and why.
activities.trySaying: "Nan's going to feel so special when she sees these."
activities.ifNotWorking: If the whisking feels hard, pre-mix the dry bits so they only stir in the wet.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child pours and stirs while you hold the bowl.
activities.makeHarder: An older one measures each part and pours the batter into rounds for you to cook.
activities.builds: Making something with your hands to give away, and meaning it.
activities.whyItWorks: Cooking for a person you love turns effort into a gift.
activities.downTheTrack: Doing kind, generous things for real people is a bond that only grows more valuable.
activities.safety: The stove and hot pan are adult-only. Wash hands and keep raw egg away from the eating bits, then wash up after cracking. Check allergies before you start.

activities.title: The waiting jelly
activities.oneLiner: Can you wait long enough for it to set?
activities.whatYouNeed: Jelly crystals, a bowl, a spoon, a fridge.
activities.getReady: You add the hot water and stir the crystals in, then let it cool a little before the child helps.
activities.howToDoIt: The child stirs, pours into cups and adds a few soft fruit bits. Then the hard part. Wait. Check it every so often to feel it going from liquid to wobble.
activities.howToGuide: Do not rush the wait. Make checking it part of the fun, not a chore.
activities.trySaying: "Not yet, let's give it more time."
activities.ifNotWorking: Set a little jelly in a shallow cup so it firms up faster to reward the wait.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child pokes it gently each check to feel the change.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses how long it will take and checks the clock.
activities.builds: Patience, and the small thrill of a reward that comes only with time.
activities.whyItWorks: A slow change you can watch makes waiting feel like doing.
activities.downTheTrack: Sitting with a wait, when everything else is instant, is a calm strength worth keeping.
activities.safety: The hot water and mixing the crystals are adult jobs. Let the mix cool before little hands help. Check allergies and use soft fruit only, cut small.

themes.bringItTogether: Across a few afternoons, smash the banana, measure the cups, taste with eyes shut, shake cream into butter, cook a gift and wait out the jelly. Every one is a tiny experiment, and your child learns the kitchen is a place where they can make things, change things and share them.

themes.title: Washing day
themes.hook: Sort, match, peg, and fold the small stuff. A basket of clean washing is a whole morning of quiet, useful play.

activities.title: Sock hunt and match
activities.oneLiner: Can you find the twin?
activities.whatYouNeed: A pile of clean, dry socks from the wash.
activities.getReady: Tip the clean socks into one big heap on the floor or the bed.
activities.howToDoIt: Dig through the heap and find pairs that match. Bundle each pair together.
activities.howToGuide: Sit back and let them scan. Resist pointing to the match.
activities.trySaying: "Whose feet do these go on?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just four socks, two easy pairs.
activities.makeEasier: Pull out three loud, different pairs to match.
activities.makeHarder: Mix in tricky near-matches, one navy and one black.
activities.builds: Slow looking, and telling near-same from truly same.
activities.whyItWorks: Sorting is quiet, careful work that rewards patience.
activities.downTheTrack: Spotting the small difference that matters is judgement no machine hands you.
activities.safety: Naming whose socks are whose builds a warm sense of family.

activities.title: Lights and darks
activities.oneLiner: Which pile does it belong in?
activities.whatYouNeed: A basket of dirty washing with no delicates, and two empty baskets.
activities.getReady: Put the two empty baskets side by side, one for lights and one for darks.
activities.howToDoIt: Pick up each item, decide light or dark, and drop it in the right basket.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose. Ask why when they are unsure, and don't correct too fast.
activities.trySaying: "Light pile or dark pile?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Hold up two clear ones first, a white singlet and black jeans.
activities.makeEasier: Sort just two groups, white and not-white.
activities.makeHarder: Add a "tricky" pile for greys and stripes to talk over.
activities.builds: Grouping the world by a rule you can see and feel.
activities.whyItWorks: Real washing has fuzzy cases, so the child has to weigh things up and decide.
activities.downTheTrack: Sorting messy things into sensible groups is thinking work that stays human.
activities.safety: Keep all detergents, powders and liquid capsules right out of reach. They poison and burn.

activities.title: Peg it on the low line
activities.oneLiner: Can you hang it so it won't blow away?
activities.whatYouNeed: Washed face washers or hankies, some pegs, and a low line or rope strung low.
activities.getReady: String a rope low between two chairs, or use the bottom rung of the clothesline.
activities.howToDoIt: Hang each small item and clip it with a peg so the breeze can't take it.
activities.howToGuide: Let them fumble the peg. It's a real hand skill worth the wobble.
activities.trySaying: "Give it a tug, will it hold?"
activities.ifNotWorking: You hold the cloth up while they push the peg.
activities.makeEasier: Use bigger, softer pegs and light little hankies.
activities.makeHarder: A whole row, evenly spaced, in a real summer breeze.
activities.builds: Small-muscle control and finishing a real outdoor job.
activities.whyItWorks: A peg that won't clip is a fiddly challenge that asks them to keep trying.
activities.downTheTrack: Patient hands that master fiddly real things keep their worth as screens do more.
activities.safety: Pegs can pinch small fingers, so try one on your own finger first to show the nip.

activities.title: Fold the little stuff
activities.oneLiner: Can you make it small and neat?
activities.whatYouNeed: Clean, dry tea towels, face washers and hankies.
activities.getReady: Smooth one flat on the table to show the shape.
activities.howToDoIt: Fold each one in half, then in half again, into a tidy square. Build a little stack.
activities.howToGuide: Fold yours slowly beside them. Let their wonky ones stand.
activities.trySaying: "Corner to corner, then press it flat."
activities.ifNotWorking: Just fold once in half and call it done.
activities.makeEasier: Start with a square face washer, the easiest for matching corners.
activities.makeHarder: Fold a T-shirt, or fold a whole stack all the same way.
activities.builds: Careful hands and steady focus on one small task.
activities.whyItWorks: Matching corners is fiddly, and the neat pile is the reward for sticking with it.
activities.downTheTrack: Finishing a thing properly, right to the last corner, is a habit worth having.
activities.safety: A wonky fold is fine. The doing is the point, not the crease.

activities.title: Wash the dolly's clothes
activities.oneLiner: Bath time for teddy's jumper?
activities.whatYouNeed: A bowl of warm water, a little mild soap, some doll clothes or a hanky, and a towel.
activities.getReady: Half fill the bowl with warm water and add a small squeeze of mild soap.
activities.howToDoIt: Swish, scrub and squeeze the clothes, then wring them out and lay them on the towel.
activities.howToGuide: Let them do the swishing. Notice together how the water changes colour.
activities.trySaying: "Where does the dirt go?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just let them splash and squeeze, no scrubbing needed.
activities.makeEasier: One hanky and lots of bubbles to play in.
activities.makeHarder: Rinse in clean water too, then peg it on the low line to dry.
activities.builds: Doing a whole real job from start to finish, on their own.
activities.whyItWorks: Watching dirty water tell its story feeds the "why does that happen" itch.
activities.downTheTrack: The belief "I can do it myself" is the root of every hard thing they will try.
activities.safety: Use only water and a little mild soap on anything a child washes, never laundry detergent, and stay within arm's reach of the water.

activities.title: Deliver the folded piles
activities.oneLiner: Special delivery, who does this belong to?
activities.whatYouNeed: The folded, sorted washing in little piles.
activities.getReady: Make a pile for each person in the house.
activities.howToDoIt: Be the postie. Carry each pile to the right person's room and leave it neatly.
activities.howToGuide: Let them work out whose is whose. Play along with the delivery game.
activities.trySaying: "Knock knock, washing delivery!"
activities.ifNotWorking: Do one delivery together, then let them try the next one alone.
activities.makeEasier: Deliver just their own pile to their own room.
activities.makeHarder: Remember every family member's room with no reminders.
activities.builds: Thinking about other people and their things, and inventing a role to do it.
activities.whyItWorks: The postie game turns a chore into a story they get to lead.
activities.downTheTrack: Caring about the people around you is the one job that is only ever ours.
activities.safety: Helping the whole household teaches that a home runs on everyone pitching in.

themes.bringItTogether: A basket of washing is sorting, matching, fiddly hands and a helping heart all in one, and by the end the little one has run a real household task from heap to happy delivery.

themes.title: Boxes and cardboard
themes.hook: Build a whole world from a big box. One empty carton becomes a cubby, a rocket, a post box and a place with its own name.

activities.title: Turn the box into a cubby
activities.oneLiner: What could this big box become?
activities.whatYouNeed: One big cardboard box, a blanket, some cushions.
activities.getReady: An adult opens or trims the box with scissors, folds down sharp corners and checks for staples.
activities.howToDoIt: Climb in and turn it into a cubby, a cave or a shop. Add a blanket for a roof.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what it is, then follow their idea rather than yours.
activities.trySaying: "What kind of place is this going to be?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Sit in it together and pretend to have a cuppa.
activities.makeEasier: A smaller box just for teddy to live in.
activities.makeHarder: Join two boxes into a tunnel and a room.
activities.builds: Seeing a plain thing and making it into something with your hands.
activities.whyItWorks: An empty box is nothing until they decide what it is, so they get to lead.
activities.downTheTrack: Turning "nothing much" into something is the maker's habit a machine can't start for you.
activities.safety: An adult does all the cutting. Never put a box over a child's head or face, and mind sharp corners and staples.

activities.title: Build the controls
activities.oneLiner: Where's the steering wheel?
activities.whatYouNeed: Bottle lids, sticky tape, a paper plate, some textas.
activities.getReady: Gather odds and ends that could be buttons, dials and a wheel.
activities.howToDoIt: Tape a paper-plate wheel and lid buttons inside the box. Now it drives or flies.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what each button does. Let their answers be the rules.
activities.trySaying: "What happens when you press that one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Draw one big red button and press it together with a sound.
activities.makeEasier: Just tape on three lids and name them go, stop and beep.
activities.makeHarder: Give every button a job and a made-up sound to match.
activities.builds: Inventing how a made-up machine works and why.
activities.whyItWorks: A button that does whatever they say feeds endless "what if" questions.
activities.downTheTrack: Asking "what could this do?" is the spark behind every new idea.
activities.safety: Bottle lids and small pins are choking hazards, so keep them well out of reach of a younger sibling.

activities.title: Cut a peephole
activities.oneLiner: Who can you spy through the little window?
activities.whatYouNeed: The box, a texta, and an adult with scissors.
activities.getReady: The child marks where a window should go and the adult cuts the flap.
activities.howToDoIt: Open and shut the flap. Peep out, spot things, and keep watch from inside.
activities.howToGuide: Go quiet together and see what you both notice through the hole.
activities.trySaying: "Ssh, what can you see out there?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the hole bigger so it's easy to see through.
activities.makeEasier: One big window at their eye height.
activities.makeHarder: Add a few peepholes and a flap that really opens and shuts.
activities.builds: Quiet noticing and watching the world go by.
activities.whyItWorks: A little window frames the world so small eyes slow down and look.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing what's really there, calmly, is attention the feed keeps trying to steal.
activities.safety: Only the adult uses the scissors, and everyone minds the cut edges.

activities.title: The cardboard post box
activities.oneLiner: Got any letters to post?
activities.whatYouNeed: A box with a slot cut by an adult, some paper, textas.
activities.getReady: The adult cuts a letter slot in the top or the side.
activities.howToDoIt: Draw letters for people you love, post them, then be the postie who delivers.
activities.howToGuide: Let their scribbles be the message. Ask who each one is for.
activities.trySaying: "Who shall we write to today?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Post leaves or bottle lids instead of letters.
activities.makeEasier: Post scribbles to Nan and Pop.
activities.makeHarder: "Write" a few letters, remember who each one is for, and deliver them all.
activities.builds: Thinking of people you love and making them something.
activities.whyItWorks: Filling and emptying the post box is a happy loop they will repeat and repeat.
activities.downTheTrack: Reaching out to people you care about is warmth that stays ours to give.
activities.safety: Drawing for someone real is an early taste of writing to connect.

activities.title: What fits and what rolls
activities.oneLiner: Will it fit? Will it roll down?
activities.whatYouNeed: A flap of cardboard for a ramp, toy cars, a ball, some blocks, and the box.
activities.getReady: Lean a cardboard flap against the couch to make a ramp.
activities.howToDoIt: Guess what fits in the box and what rolls down the ramp, then test each one.
activities.howToGuide: Let them guess first, then find out. The wrong guesses are the good bit.
activities.trySaying: "Do you reckon it'll roll or stop?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just roll cars down and cheer the fast ones.
activities.makeEasier: Roll round things and drop them in the box.
activities.makeHarder: Line up which rolls fastest and why, then tilt the ramp steeper.
activities.builds: Testing a hunch against what really happens.
activities.whyItWorks: A guess that's wrong is a small surprise that makes them want another go.
activities.downTheTrack: Checking whether a thing is actually true, not just told to you, is the skill of the age.
activities.safety: Guessing then checking is the heart of how little kids learn what's true.

activities.title: Name and paint the world
activities.oneLiner: What shall we call this place?
activities.whatYouNeed: Textas, crayons, the finished box world, some scrap paper.
activities.getReady: Lay out the drawing gear near the box.
activities.howToDoIt: Decorate the box, give the place a name, and add who lives there.
activities.howToGuide: Their name and their colours win, even the odd ones.
activities.trySaying: "You're the boss of this place, what's it called?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just add one door and one window and call it home.
activities.makeEasier: Scribble a splash of colour and call it done.
activities.makeHarder: Draw the people who live there and a sign with the name on it.
activities.builds: Owning a project and putting your own stamp on it.
activities.whyItWorks: Naming and decorating slows them right down to add the little details.
activities.downTheTrack: Making something yours, then sharing it, is a joy no device can hand you.
activities.safety: When the box is finally done with, an adult flattens it for the recycling.

themes.bringItTogether: One big box carries a whole day, from building and inventing to quiet watching, careful testing and a place with its own name, and the little one gets to be the maker, the pilot, the postie and the boss of it all.

themes.title: Sounds of the House
themes.hook: Listen, find, name and copy the noises. The house is full of little sounds waiting to be noticed.

activities.title: Sound detective
activities.oneLiner: How many sounds can you catch just by sitting still?
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing at all. Maybe a cushion each.
activities.getReady: Turn off the telly and any music so the quiet has room.
activities.howToDoIt: Sit close together, stay still, and count the sounds you catch. The fridge humming. A magpie warbling outside. Your own tummy. Hold up a finger for each new one.
activities.howToGuide: Stay quiet yourself and let them find sounds you missed. Do not name them all first.
activities.trySaying: "Shh, what can you hear right now?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with your eyes closed for ten seconds, then open and compare.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just points at where a sound is coming from.
activities.makeHarder: An older one sorts sounds into near ones and far ones.
activities.builds: The knack of holding still and paying real attention.
activities.whyItWorks: Naming near from far is small, honest judgement about the world.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing what is really there, when machines will happily fill the quiet for us.
activities.safety: Little ears are sensitive, so keep the room calm and never test them with anything loud.

activities.title: Kitchen taps
activities.oneLiner: Which spoon sings the highest note?
activities.whatYouNeed: A wooden spoon and a few safe kitchen things like an upturned bowl, a saucepan, a plastic tub, a cushion.
activities.getReady: Line the objects up on the floor where nobody can trip. Keep the tapping gentle and well away from ears.
activities.howToDoIt: Give each object a soft tap and listen. Which one is deep? Which one is high? Which one goes thud and makes no note at all?
activities.howToGuide: Ask before you answer. Let them tap and decide for themselves.
activities.trySaying: "Was that one higher or lower?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just tap two very different things, like the pot and the cushion, and feel the difference.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child bangs softly and enjoys the noise.
activities.makeHarder: An older one lines the objects up from lowest note to highest.
activities.builds: Hands-on know-how, learning that different stuff makes different sounds.
activities.whyItWorks: Testing and comparing is the start of asking why.
activities.downTheTrack: Curiosity you act on with your own hands, not just questions you type in.
activities.safety: No knives, no glass, and only ever a soft tap. Loud clangs near little ears can hurt them.

activities.title: Animal copycats
activities.oneLiner: Can you fool your mum with a kookaburra laugh?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just your voices.
activities.getReady: Think of a few Aussie animals you both know. A kookaburra, a magpie, a frog, a cockatoo, a possum on the roof at night.
activities.howToDoIt: Take turns making the sound. The other one guesses which animal it is, then has a go too.
activities.howToGuide: Let their version be their own. There is no wrong kookaburra.
activities.trySaying: "You be the animal, I'll guess."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with an easy one you both know well, like a barking dog.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child copies the sound you make.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes up a call for a made-up creature and describes it.
activities.builds: Making a sound your own way and being brave enough to perform it.
activities.whyItWorks: Pretending to be something else is imagination doing real work.
activities.downTheTrack: The confidence to make something and put it out there, which no tool hands you.
activities.safety: Cockatoos are loud in real life, so keep your indoor version soft and kind on the ears.

activities.title: Guess who said hello
activities.oneLiner: Can you tell your family just by their voice?
activities.whatYouNeed: A tea towel or scarf for a blindfold, and a couple of family members or friends nearby.
activities.getReady: Gather two or three people who are happy to join in.
activities.howToDoIt: The child closes their eyes or wears the blindfold. One person says "hello" in their normal voice. Can the child guess who it was? Swap around.
activities.howToGuide: Let them listen properly before they answer. Do not rush the guess.
activities.trySaying: "Whose voice was that one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Have each person say hello once with eyes open first, so the child links voice to face.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child guesses between just two people.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses when the person whispers or talks in a funny voice.
activities.builds: Tuning in to the people around you and holding your focus on them.
activities.whyItWorks: A voice carries who someone is, and noticing that is caring attention.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading real people well, when plenty of voices out there will be made by machines.
activities.safety: We know the people we love partly by the sound of them, and this quietly names that.

activities.title: Mystery shaker
activities.oneLiner: What is rattling around inside?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clean empty jar or bottle with a lid, and big safe fillers like a large pasta shell, a wine cork, a big wooden bead, a metal spoon.
activities.getReady: Choose fillers that are far too big to swallow. Pop one kind inside and screw the lid on tight. Tape it shut for extra safety.
activities.howToDoIt: Give the sealed shaker a gentle shake and listen. Is it a rattle, a thud, a jingle? Can they guess what is inside before you open it?
activities.howToGuide: Let them shake and think before you reveal it. Wondering is the fun part.
activities.trySaying: "What do you reckon is making that sound?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Show them the two choices first, then close the jar and let them pick by ear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just enjoys shaking and you name what is inside together.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses how many things are inside from the sound.
activities.builds: Sticking with a puzzle you cannot see into, and testing ideas by hand.
activities.whyItWorks: A hidden thing you can only hear is a proper little mystery to solve.
activities.downTheTrack: Patience with a problem that does not answer straight away.
activities.safety: Only ever use items too big to swallow, and always seal the lid shut. Keep the shake soft and away from ears.

activities.title: Loud, soft, real or silly
activities.oneLiner: Which sounds are real, and which ones did we make up?
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing, or scrap paper and a pencil to jot a list.
activities.getReady: Walk slowly through one or two rooms together, listening as you go.
activities.howToDoIt: Find real house sounds like a tap dripping or the wind at the window. Then invent a silly sound of your own. Sort them out loud into real ones and made-up ones.
activities.howToGuide: Let the child decide which pile a sound goes in, even if you would choose differently.
activities.trySaying: "Is that a real sound or a made-up one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Do just two, one clearly real and one clearly silly, and talk about the difference.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child points to loud sounds and soft sounds.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes a sound effect for a small story you tell together.
activities.builds: Judgement about what is real, plus the fun of inventing your own.
activities.whyItWorks: Sorting real from made-up is the same muscle we use to sniff out a fib.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling true from fake, which matters more as machines learn to fake sound.
activities.safety: Telling real from pretend is a real skill, and doing it with sounds makes it playful.

themes.bringItTogether: Over a week you have sat still and listened, tapped and compared, copied and invented, and told the real from the made-up. That is the whole loop of a good listener, and your child grew it with their own ears.

themes.title: Mirrors and Reflections
themes.hook: Faces, light, and what bounces back. A mirror is a small window into how the world reflects.

activities.title: Mirror copycat
activities.oneLiner: Can you two move exactly the same?
activities.whatYouNeed: A well-secured mirror on a wall, or an unbreakable mirror.
activities.getReady: Stand together where you can both see the mirror. Never let a little one carry glass.
activities.howToDoIt: Pull a face and hold it. Now they copy it back. Slow smile, big yawn, cheeky wink. Then swap, and you copy them.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their face as much as you lead. Let them be the boss sometimes.
activities.trySaying: "Now you make the face and I'll copy."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just a big smile and a big frown.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child copies one clear face at a time.
activities.makeHarder: An older one copies a whole little sequence of three faces in order.
activities.builds: Tuning in to another person's face and holding your focus on it.
activities.whyItWorks: Copying a face is how babies first learn to read feelings, and it still works.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading a real human face, a thing screens flatten and machines only imitate.
activities.safety: For little ones use a mirror fixed to the wall or an unbreakable one, and keep all glass out of their hands.

activities.title: Shiny thing hunt
activities.oneLiner: What else in the house can act like a mirror?
activities.whatYouNeed: A metal spoon, some foil, a window at dusk, a bowl of water, anything that might reflect.
activities.getReady: Gather a few shiny and dull things on a table to compare.
activities.howToDoIt: Look for your face or the light in each object. Which ones reflect clearly? Which ones are a bit blurry? Which do not reflect at all?
activities.howToGuide: Let them test each thing and decide. Ask what makes some things reflect and others not.
activities.trySaying: "Can you find your face in that one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with the shiny spoon next to a tea towel, a clear yes and a clear no.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts things into shiny and not shiny.
activities.makeHarder: An older one notices the spoon flips your face upside down on one side.
activities.builds: Curiosity you follow around the house, plus judging what reflects and what does not.
activities.whyItWorks: Sorting real reflections from dull surfaces is small, careful looking.
activities.downTheTrack: Testing things yourself rather than taking the first easy answer.
activities.safety: Never reflect the sun into anyone's eyes, and keep glass mirrors out of little hands.

activities.title: Fold-and-print butterfly
activities.oneLiner: Can you make two sides match exactly?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, washable paint or textas, and a flat table.
activities.getReady: Fold a sheet of paper in half and open it flat. Lay down some newspaper to catch the mess.
activities.howToDoIt: Blob paint on one side of the fold only. Fold it shut, press and smooth it, then open it up. The two sides mirror each other, like butterfly wings.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose the colours and where the blobs go. The surprise on opening is the joy.
activities.trySaying: "Let's see what the other side did."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use just one big blob of one colour so the mirror effect is clear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child presses the fold while you place the paint.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plans blobs to make a proper butterfly or a face.
activities.builds: Making something new, and handling real paint and paper to do it.
activities.whyItWorks: Watching one side become two is a hands-on lesson in how a mirror works.
activities.downTheTrack: The maker's habit of trying a thing and seeing what comes out.
activities.safety: This shows symmetry, which is the same idea a mirror makes. Use old clothes.

activities.title: Backwards writing
activities.oneLiner: Why does the mirror flip your name around?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, a thick pencil or texta, and a secured or unbreakable mirror.
activities.getReady: Write the child's first initial big on the paper. Have the mirror standing steady.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold the letter up to the mirror. See how it flips? Now try drawing it backwards on purpose so it looks right in the mirror. Tricky.
activities.howToGuide: Let them puzzle over why it flips. Do not fix their backwards letters, that is the point.
activities.trySaying: "What did the mirror do to your letter?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just hold up a simple shape like an arrow and watch it point the other way.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child waves a toy at the mirror and watches the copy wave back.
activities.makeHarder: An older one writes a short word and reads it back to front in the mirror.
activities.builds: Noticing that a mirror changes things, and sticking with a properly fiddly task.
activities.whyItWorks: A flipped letter shows a mirror does not just copy, it reverses.
activities.downTheTrack: Looking twice at what seems obvious, and not giving up when it is hard.
activities.safety: Keep the mirror secured or unbreakable, and never let the child carry it about.

activities.title: Sky in a puddle
activities.oneLiner: Can you find the clouds down low?
activities.whatYouNeed: A dark bowl or bucket of water, or a still puddle after rain.
activities.getReady: Set the bowl on the ground outside in an open spot. Winter mornings are good for still, bright skies.
activities.howToDoIt: Look down into the water and find the sky reflected there. Watch clouds drift across it. Drop in one leaf and see the whole sky wobble.
activities.howToGuide: Stay quiet and let them watch. Let them be the one to spot a passing bird overhead in the water.
activities.trySaying: "Look, the sky is down in the water."
activities.ifNotWorking: Wait for a moment with no wind so the water sits perfectly still.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child pats the water and watches it break the picture.
activities.makeHarder: An older one works out why the reflection turns everything upside down.
activities.builds: Quiet watching, and wondering how the sky ended up on the ground.
activities.whyItWorks: A still surface reflecting the sky is nature's own mirror, free and huge.
activities.downTheTrack: The patience to watch and wonder, a calm that fast screens rarely allow.
activities.safety: Never leave a young child alone near any water, even a shallow bowl.

activities.title: Bounce the light
activities.oneLiner: Can you send a spot of light around the room?
activities.whatYouNeed: A torch, and a spoon, foil or a small secured mirror.
activities.getReady: Dim the room. Sit on the floor so the reflector points at a wall, not at faces.
activities.howToDoIt: Shine the torch onto the shiny surface and catch the bright spot on the wall. Now tilt it and make the spot travel, climb, hide behind the couch.
activities.howToGuide: Let them hold the torch and steer. Let them set where the light should go.
activities.trySaying: "Can you make the light climb up to the ceiling?"
activities.ifNotWorking: You hold the mirror steady while they aim the torch, then swap.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just chases the spot you make with their hand.
activities.makeHarder: An older one bounces the light off two surfaces to reach a target.
activities.builds: Believing you can steer the light, using real gear to do it, and inventing where it goes.
activities.whyItWorks: Aiming a bounced beam shows light travels and turns, and that they can control it.
activities.downTheTrack: The doer's belief that you can act on the world and make it move.
activities.safety: Never shine the torch or a reflection into anyone's eyes, and never use the sun to do this.

themes.bringItTogether: Across these you have copied faces, hunted reflections, folded symmetry, flipped letters, found the sky in a puddle, and steered light with your own hand. Mirrors quietly taught your child that the world bounces back, and that they can play with how it does.

themes.title: My amazing body
themes.hook: Hands, feet, and all five senses. Six gentle ways to help your child fall in love with the body that is theirs, and theirs alone.

activities.title: Mystery smell jars
activities.oneLiner: Can your nose work out what's hiding?
activities.whatYouNeed: Three or four small cups, and smelly things from the kitchen like coffee, orange peel, mint, vanilla.
activities.getReady: Pop one thing in each cup while they look away.
activities.howToDoIt: They close their eyes, take a sniff, and have a guess.
activities.howToGuide: Wait through the pause. A good guess takes a think.
activities.trySaying: "What does that one remind you of?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Show them the things first, then hide just one.
activities.makeEasier: Use big obvious smells like orange and coffee.
activities.makeHarder: Try two soft smells that are easy to muddle, like vanilla and honey.
activities.builds: Trusting your own nose to tell one thing from another.
activities.whyItWorks: Naming a smell means sorting it from every other smell you know.
activities.downTheTrack: Weighing the evidence and backing your own judgement, which no machine can do for them.
activities.safety: Nothing goes up the nose, just a sniff from above. Skip anything they are allergic to.

activities.title: Barefoot texture path
activities.oneLiner: What can your feet feel that your eyes can't?
activities.whatYouNeed: A patch of lawn, some smooth pavers, a towel, maybe a tray of sand or dry rice.
activities.getReady: Lay a few different surfaces in a row.
activities.howToDoIt: Walk the path slowly with bare feet and notice each one.
activities.howToGuide: Let them set the pace and stop where they like.
activities.trySaying: "Which bit feels the best under your toes?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Hold their hand and walk it together the first time.
activities.makeEasier: Just grass and a soft towel to start.
activities.makeHarder: Add a cool step and a warm one, and see if they can feel the change.
activities.builds: Reading the real world through the soles of your feet.
activities.whyItWorks: Slow bare feet notice what shoes and rushing hide.
activities.downTheTrack: Paying close attention to the physical world, a skill screens can never hand them.
activities.safety: Check the ground for sharp bits and bindies before they step on.

activities.title: My yes, my no
activities.oneLiner: Who gets to say when the tickles stop?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just the two of you.
activities.getReady: Sit somewhere comfy and cosy.
activities.howToDoIt: Play gentle tickle games, and the second they say stop, you stop straight away.
activities.howToGuide: Make a big warm deal of listening the instant they ask.
activities.trySaying: "Your body, your choice. You tell me."
activities.ifNotWorking: Swap to something they do want, like a cuddle they ask for.
activities.makeEasier: Use one clear word like stop or a raised hand.
activities.makeHarder: Let them run the game and tell you where a tickle is okay and where it isn't.
activities.builds: Knowing your no matters and will be heard.
activities.whyItWorks: When stop really stops, a child learns their voice has power.
activities.downTheTrack: Standing up for yourself and reading how others feel, the heart of every human team.
activities.safety: Their body belongs to them. Saying yes or no to touch is always their call.

activities.title: Hand shadow creatures
activities.oneLiner: What can two hands turn into on the wall?
activities.whatYouNeed: A torch or lamp, and a blank wall in a dim room.
activities.getReady: Point the light at the wall and dim the others.
activities.howToDoIt: Twist your fingers into a dog, a bird, a snapping crocodile.
activities.howToGuide: Show one, then let them invent their own.
activities.trySaying: "What could your hands become next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with a flapping bird, the easiest shape to make.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child makes any shape and names it whatever they like.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes a little story with two creatures talking.
activities.builds: Making something new out of nothing but fingers and light.
activities.whyItWorks: A shape that won't hold takes a few tries to get right.
activities.downTheTrack: Inventing, and staying with a fiddly job, both worth more as the easy jobs vanish.
activities.safety: Small hands tire fast, so keep it short and silly.

activities.title: Feel your heartbeat
activities.oneLiner: Can you hear your own engine speed up?
activities.whatYouNeed: A hand, and a bit of space to jump.
activities.getReady: Rest a hand flat on the chest and go quiet.
activities.howToDoIt: Feel the slow beat, do ten star jumps, then feel it race.
activities.howToGuide: Let them make the discovery, don't tell them the answer first.
activities.trySaying: "What happened to your heart when you jumped?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Feel your heartbeat too so they know what to hunt for.
activities.makeEasier: Just jump and giggle, and feel the puff in your chest.
activities.makeHarder: Guess whether hopping or running makes it beat faster, then test it.
activities.builds: Noticing your own body change and wondering why.
activities.whyItWorks: A racing heart is proof they can feel, a question they can chase.
activities.downTheTrack: Asking why and testing it yourself, the curiosity that keeps learning alive for life.
activities.safety: A quick heartbeat after moving is healthy and normal. Let them rest when they want.

activities.title: Sound detective
activities.oneLiner: Where in the room is that little noise?
activities.whatYouNeed: A ticking timer, a phone alarm, or a set of keys.
activities.getReady: Hide the sound somewhere in the room while they cover their eyes.
activities.howToDoIt: They open their eyes and follow their ears to find it.
activities.howToGuide: Let them turn their head and listen, don't point.
activities.trySaying: "Is it closer, or further away?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the sound louder, or hide it in plain sight.
activities.makeEasier: Hide it just behind you so it's an easy first win.
activities.makeHarder: Hide two soft sounds and see if they can tell them apart.
activities.builds: Holding your focus on one small sound in a busy room.
activities.whyItWorks: Finding a sound means sorting it out from all the others.
activities.downTheTrack: Filtering the signal from the noise, the rare focus a distracting world keeps chipping at.
activities.safety: Quiet homes make this easier, so switch the telly off.

themes.bringItTogether: Six ways to say the same warm thing. This body is amazing, it is yours, and you are the boss of it.

themes.title: Balance and wobble
themes.hook: Beams, one-leg games, and careful carrying. Six low and steady ways to help your child find their feet, always near the ground and always in reach.

activities.title: Walk the line
activities.oneLiner: Can you follow the rope without falling off?
activities.whatYouNeed: A length of rope, or a strip of masking tape, laid flat on the floor.
activities.getReady: Lay it in a straight line, then add a wiggle or two.
activities.howToDoIt: Walk heel to toe along the line, arms out like a plane.
activities.howToGuide: Stay within arm's reach, but let them find their own balance.
activities.trySaying: "Eyes forward, and take your time."
activities.ifNotWorking: Hold one hand for the first walk, then let go.
activities.makeEasier: A wide painted line they just step along.
activities.makeHarder: Walk it backwards, or balance a soft toy on one hand.
activities.builds: Steering your own body along a path you can see.
activities.whyItWorks: A wobble is instant feedback that tells them to adjust.
activities.downTheTrack: Backing yourself to have a go, the quiet confidence that starts everything.
activities.safety: Keep it flat on the floor with nothing hard nearby to knock into.

activities.title: Flamingo contest
activities.oneLiner: How long can you stand like a flamingo?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just two legs and a soft floor.
activities.getReady: Clear a bit of space with a rug or grass underfoot.
activities.howToDoIt: Lift one foot, count together, and see how long you last.
activities.howToGuide: Cheer the trying, not just the record.
activities.trySaying: "One more second, you've got this."
activities.ifNotWorking: Let them rest a hand on a wall or on you.
activities.makeEasier: Just lift a heel off the ground for a moment.
activities.makeHarder: Close your eyes, or hold a spoon out steady while you stand.
activities.builds: Staying with the wobble instead of giving up on it.
activities.whyItWorks: Each wobbly try tells them where their balance lives.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with something hard past the first fail, which is where real skill is made.
activities.safety: Soft ground underneath, and stay close in case they topple.

activities.title: Careful carry
activities.oneLiner: Can you cross the room without a single drop?
activities.whatYouNeed: A spoon and a pompom, or a small cup with a little water.
activities.getReady: Mark a start line and a finish with two cushions.
activities.howToDoIt: Carry the spoon across, slow and steady, without dropping the load.
activities.howToGuide: Bite your tongue when it wobbles, let them fix it.
activities.trySaying: "Slow feet, steady hands."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a bigger spoon and a lighter load like a cotton ball.
activities.makeEasier: Carry it a short step, then build the distance.
activities.makeHarder: A fuller cup, or a wiggly path between cushions.
activities.builds: Handling a real object with real care.
activities.whyItWorks: Every step is a small choice between rushing and holding steady.
activities.downTheTrack: Doing a careful job with your hands, the kind of steady competence machines can't fake.
activities.safety: Water on the floor is slippery, so mop up little spills as you go.

activities.title: Beanbag balance
activities.oneLiner: Can you be still enough to keep it on your head?
activities.whatYouNeed: A beanbag, a folded flannel, or a small soft toy.
activities.getReady: Clear a soft, open patch of floor.
activities.howToDoIt: Balance it on your head and move like a robot, a cat, a sleepy giant.
activities.howToGuide: Let them pick the character and how slow to go.
activities.trySaying: "How still do you need to be for this one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start by just standing still with it, no walking.
activities.makeEasier: Balance it on a flat hand instead of a head.
activities.makeHarder: Squat down and stand back up without it sliding off.
activities.builds: Judging just how much to move before it slips.
activities.whyItWorks: They pretend and read their own body at the same time.
activities.downTheTrack: Making up your own play, and reading a situation before you act on it.
activities.safety: Soft item only, and clear the floor of anything to trip on.

activities.title: Stepping stones
activities.oneLiner: Can you cross the river without touching the water?
activities.whatYouNeed: A few flat cushions or folded towels.
activities.getReady: Space them a small, safe step apart on the floor.
activities.howToDoIt: Hop or step from cushion to cushion across the pretend river.
activities.howToGuide: Let them plan their own route across.
activities.trySaying: "Which stone will you step to next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Move the cushions closer so every step feels safe.
activities.makeEasier: Big cushions right beside each other.
activities.makeHarder: Spread them a touch wider, or add a slow motion crossing.
activities.builds: Choosing your own path and trusting your feet to follow it.
activities.whyItWorks: They read the gaps and decide, then their body carries out the plan.
activities.downTheTrack: Planning a route and acting on it yourself, the doer's mindset that gets things done.
activities.safety: Keep cushions flat and low on a non-slip floor, and stay within reach.

activities.title: Mirror wobbles
activities.oneLiner: Can you copy my balance without a peek at your feet?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just the two of you, facing each other.
activities.getReady: Stand an arm's length apart on soft ground.
activities.howToDoIt: You strike a balance, they mirror it, then they lead and you follow.
activities.howToGuide: Watch their face, and match your speed to theirs.
activities.trySaying: "You be the leader now, I'll copy you."
activities.ifNotWorking: Try easy poses first, like both arms up high.
activities.makeEasier: Sit down and mirror just arm shapes.
activities.makeHarder: Add a one-leg pose, or a slow wobble they have to match.
activities.builds: Tuning in to another person and moving with them.
activities.whyItWorks: Copying a body means watching it closely and wondering how it moves.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading and working alongside other people, the skill that only grows more precious.
activities.safety: Soft ground, low poses, and a hand ready if either of you tips.

themes.bringItTogether: Every wobble is the body learning. Stay low, stay close, and let them find their own steady feet.

themes.title: Fast and slow
themes.hook: Race, freeze, tiptoe, and control the body. Six little games that teach a small child the quiet power to speed up, slow down and stop on purpose.

activities.title: Freeze like a statue
activities.oneLiner: Can you stop dead the very second you hear "freeze"?
activities.whatYouNeed: A bit of open lawn and your voices.
activities.getReady: Pick a start line and a finish line a good run apart.
activities.howToDoIt: Call "green" and they run toward you, call "red" and they freeze. Anyone still wobbling takes a step back.
activities.howToGuide: Resist calling the wobble every time. Let them feel their own body settle.
activities.trySaying: "Can you freeze before I finish saying it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Slow your calls right down and make the freezes short.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child walks instead of runs.
activities.makeHarder: An older child freezes in a silly shape and holds it.
activities.builds: Holding still on command is attention you can feel.
activities.whyItWorks: The gap between "red" and stopping is self-control being built.
activities.downTheTrack: Steering your own focus on and off is a human superpower no app can hand over.
activities.safety: Run only on open grass clear of roads, corners and water, keep eyes up so no one collides, and stop for a drink.

activities.title: Fast feet, slow feet
activities.oneLiner: Your feet copy the drum, quick when it's quick, slow when it's slow.
activities.whatYouNeed: A saucepan and a wooden spoon, or just your hands to clap.
activities.getReady: Clear a little path to march along.
activities.howToDoIt: Tap a beat and they step in time. Speed it up, slow it down, and see if their feet follow.
activities.howToGuide: Watch their feet, not their face. Give them a beat they can actually catch.
activities.trySaying: "Are my taps fast or slow right now?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use only two speeds, very fast and very slow, nothing in between.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child claps hands instead of stepping.
activities.makeHarder: An older child leads the drum while you march.
activities.builds: Telling quick from slow is the first sorting a mind does.
activities.whyItWorks: Matching feet to a beat trains the ear and the body to agree.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading a signal and judging your response is thinking, not just reacting.
activities.safety: Naming fast and slow gives them the words for comparing and judging.

activities.title: Beat the timer, then beat it slow
activities.oneLiner: How fast can you fill the basket, and how gently can you empty it?
activities.whatYouNeed: A laundry basket, a pile of washing or soft toys, a timer.
activities.getReady: Scatter the soft things around one room.
activities.howToDoIt: First round, race the timer to gather everything. Second round, put each thing back as slowly and carefully as you can.
activities.howToGuide: Let them set their own pace on the slow round. Don't hurry them.
activities.trySaying: "You did the whole job yourself."
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop the timer and just race your parent instead.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child carries one thing at a time.
activities.makeHarder: An older child sorts as they go, socks here, toys there.
activities.builds: A real job finished by their own hands.
activities.whyItWorks: Fast then slow shows them they can control effort, not just have it.
activities.downTheTrack: Knowing you can start and finish a real task is confidence machines can't gift you.
activities.safety: Real chores done at speed and then with care build true competence.

activities.title: Tiptoe past the sleeping bear
activities.oneLiner: Can you sneak past without waking the snoozing bear?
activities.whatYouNeed: A parent or a big teddy to be the bear.
activities.getReady: One person lies down as the sleeping bear at the far end.
activities.howToDoIt: Everyone tiptoes toward the bear. If the bear stirs, freeze. Get close enough to gently tag it and the bear wakes with a friendly roar.
activities.howToGuide: Play the bear warmly. Read whether they want a big roar or a soft one.
activities.trySaying: "Shh, is the bear still sleeping?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the bear a very heavy sleeper who barely moves.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child holds your hand as you creep.
activities.makeHarder: An older child crosses a floor of "crackly" cushions without a sound.
activities.builds: Moving softly for someone else's sake is early empathy.
activities.whyItWorks: They watch the bear closely and adjust, which is connection in action.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading a person and responding with care is the work AI keeps failing at.
activities.safety: Tuning their body to someone else's builds care and reading people.

activities.title: How slow can you go
activities.oneLiner: The winner is the last one to cross the line, so how slow can you go?
activities.whatYouNeed: Two lines marked with sticks or shoes, a short way apart.
activities.getReady: Set a start and finish only a few steps apart.
activities.howToDoIt: Everyone moves in the slowest slow motion. You must keep moving, no stopping. Last to reach the line wins.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder aloud about how to move slower. Let them experiment.
activities.trySaying: "I wonder how slow a foot can move?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Race to be slowest over just one giant step.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child does one slow-motion arm wave.
activities.makeHarder: An older child balances on one slow leg mid-step.
activities.builds: Holding back speed is patience the body can feel.
activities.whyItWorks: Slowest wins flips the game and makes them curious about control.
activities.downTheTrack: Patience and the urge to experiment are what turn a question into an answer.
activities.safety: Going slow on purpose takes more patience than going fast.

activities.title: Musical statues with a feeling
activities.oneLiner: When the music stops, freeze in a feeling and let us guess it.
activities.whatYouNeed: A phone or radio for music you can start and stop.
activities.getReady: Choose a song and clear a dancing space.
activities.howToDoIt: Dance fast to the fast bits, sway to the slow bits. When you pause the music they freeze showing a feeling, happy, sleepy, grumpy. Everyone guesses.
activities.howToGuide: Guess their feeling out loud and let them tell you if you're right.
activities.trySaying: "What feeling is that statue showing?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Give them one feeling to try before the music starts.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child copies your frozen feeling.
activities.makeHarder: An older child shows a feeling with no face, only their body.
activities.builds: Showing a feeling with the body is imagination made visible.
activities.whyItWorks: Reading and guessing feelings joins creativity to caring.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling one feeling from another is judgement about people, and that stays valuable however work changes.
activities.safety: Dance in a space clear of corners and hard edges, and keep eyes up.

themes.bringItTogether: Fast, freeze, tiptoe and slow are all the same skill wearing different clothes, the quiet power to run your own body and mind on purpose.

themes.title: Colours
themes.hook: Hunt them, mix them, sort the world by them. Six little activities that turn colour from something a small child just sees into something they notice, make and think about.

activities.title: One-colour treasure hunt
activities.oneLiner: Can you find five things in the garden that are all the same colour?
activities.whatYouNeed: An egg carton or a small bag, and one colour chosen together.
activities.getReady: Pick a colour and find one example to start them off.
activities.howToDoIt: Hunt the yard or park for things of that colour and collect the safe ones.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide if a thing counts. Ask why they think it matches.
activities.trySaying: "Is that the same red as our first one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Widen it to "anything greenish" rather than one exact shade.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child points instead of collecting.
activities.makeHarder: An older child hunts for shades, light green to dark green, and lines them up.
activities.builds: Noticing one colour everywhere sharpens the eye.
activities.whyItWorks: A hunt turns looking into a question they chase.
activities.downTheTrack: A mind that notices detail and keeps asking is one that spots what others miss.
activities.safety: Never eat foraged berries, petals or leaves, some are poisonous, and wash hands afterward.

activities.title: Mix a brand new colour
activities.oneLiner: What happens when blue meets yellow in a puddle of paint?
activities.whatYouNeed: Non-toxic paint in red, blue and yellow, a white plate, a brush.
activities.getReady: Put a blob of each colour around the edge of the plate.
activities.howToDoIt: Let them mix two colours in the middle and watch a third appear. Name the new colour together.
activities.howToGuide: Don't tell them what they'll make. Let the surprise be theirs.
activities.trySaying: "You made a colour that wasn't there before."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just blue and yellow for a clear green.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child mixes with a spoon or fingers.
activities.makeHarder: An older child tries to match a colour they can see, like a leaf.
activities.builds: Hands-on mixing shows how the world's colours are made.
activities.whyItWorks: Making a new colour from scratch is real cause and effect.
activities.downTheTrack: Understanding how things combine is the root of inventing something new.
activities.safety: Use non-toxic paint only, never eat it, and wash hands when you finish.

activities.title: Sort the odd sock basket
activities.oneLiner: Every sock has a home, can you group them by colour?
activities.whatYouNeed: A pile of clean socks, and pegs or bowls in a few colours.
activities.getReady: Tip the socks into one heap.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort them into groups by colour. Argue kindly about where the stripy ones go.
activities.howToGuide: Let them make the rules for the tricky ones. Ask them to explain.
activities.trySaying: "Where does this spotty one belong?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Sort just two colours to start.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child matches pairs instead of colour groups.
activities.makeHarder: An older child sorts by shade, light to dark.
activities.builds: Choosing a group for each sock is judgement in miniature.
activities.whyItWorks: The tricky in-between socks force a real decision.
activities.downTheTrack: Sorting the clear from the fuzzy is thinking work that stays yours.
activities.safety: Deciding what belongs where builds real judgement.

activities.title: Grow a colour garden
activities.oneLiner: Plant something and wait for its colour to arrive.
activities.time: 15 min to plant, then weeks of watching
activities.whatYouNeed: A pot, some soil, quick seeds like nasturtium or a punnet of seedlings, water.
activities.getReady: Fill the pot with soil and choose a sunny spot.
activities.howToDoIt: They plant the seeds themselves, water them, and check each day for the colour to show.
activities.howToGuide: Hand over the watering can. Let it be their plant, their job.
activities.trySaying: "This one is yours to look after."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a seedling that already has a bud so colour comes sooner.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child waters while you plant.
activities.makeHarder: An older child keeps a little tally of days until the first flower.
activities.builds: One plant, cared for daily, is agency they can hold.
activities.whyItWorks: Colour that takes weeks teaches waiting without giving up.
activities.downTheTrack: Seeing a slow thing through to the end is grit that pays off for a lifetime.
activities.safety: Wash hands after handling soil, and check the plant is non-toxic before you choose it.

activities.title: A colour card for someone you love
activities.oneLiner: Which colour says "I'm thinking of you"?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, non-toxic crayons or paint, and someone in mind.
activities.getReady: Talk about who the card is for and what colours they like.
activities.howToDoIt: Make a card in that person's favourite colours, then deliver it or post it.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what Nan loves, not what they love. Let them choose for someone else.
activities.trySaying: "What colour would make Poppy smile?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start by asking who has a favourite colour they already know.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child scribbles in the chosen colour.
activities.makeHarder: An older child writes the person's name or a small message.
activities.builds: Choosing colours for someone else is caring made into a gift.
activities.whyItWorks: Thinking about another person's taste stretches them past themselves.
activities.downTheTrack: Making something thoughtful for a real person is a warmth no machine can fake.
activities.safety: Use non-toxic materials, don't eat crayons or paint, and wash hands after.

activities.title: Real colour or trick colour?
activities.oneLiner: Is the sky really blue, or is it playing a trick?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear glass of water, a white spoon, sunshine, and your eyes.
activities.getReady: Fill a glass with water and find a sunny window or spot outside.
activities.howToDoIt: Notice how the water looks clear in the glass but the sea looks blue. Dip the spoon and watch it look bent. Wonder together about what's real and what's a trick of the light.
activities.howToGuide: Don't rush to explain. Let them guess first, then test their guess.
activities.trySaying: "Is the spoon really bent, or does it just look it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Just play with shadows changing the colour of a toy.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child spots something that changes colour in the shade.
activities.makeHarder: An older child predicts what a colour will do before you test it.
activities.builds: Testing what's real trains a careful, curious eye.
activities.whyItWorks: Noticing that seeing can fool you is the start of real discernment.
activities.downTheTrack: Asking "is that actually true?" is the exact habit that guards against being fooled.
activities.safety: Light bends and scatters, which is why deep water looks blue and a half-dipped spoon looks bent. Both are tricks of the light, not the thing itself.

themes.bringItTogether: Hunt them, mix them, sort them and question them, and colour turns from something they just see into something they notice, make and think about.

themes.title: Shapes
themes.hook: Spot them, build them, draw them everywhere.

activities.title: Shape hunt around the house
activities.oneLiner: How many circles live in your kitchen?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just your eyes and your feet.
activities.getReady: Pick one shape to hunt first, like circles.
activities.howToDoIt: Walk room to room and call out every circle you find.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their pointing instead of leading the way.
activities.trySaying: "Where's a circle hiding?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start in one small spot, like the fridge door.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child finds one big obvious circle.
activities.makeHarder: An older one hunts a shape with no straight sides at all.
activities.builds: Slowing down and really noticing what is already around you.
activities.whyItWorks: The house turns into a puzzle they solve with their eyes.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing small details is a human edge that machines still miss.
activities.safety: Clock faces, plug holes and buttons are all circles, so it is everywhere once you look.

activities.title: Build a shape with playdough snakes
activities.oneLiner: Can you make a triangle out of three snakes?
activities.whatYouNeed: Playdough or homemade dough, a flat table.
activities.getReady: Roll a couple of long snakes together first.
activities.howToDoIt: Bend and join the snakes into squares, triangles and stars.
activities.howToGuide: Let them squash it and start again as often as they like.
activities.trySaying: "How many sides does that one need?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make one snake yourself and let them add the next.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child presses dough into a cutter shape.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds a shape standing up off the table.
activities.builds: Turning a shape in their head into a thing their hands can hold.
activities.whyItWorks: A wobbly square teaches corners far better than a picture ever could.
activities.downTheTrack: Making real things with your hands stays valuable when screens do the rest.
activities.safety: Homemade dough is flour, salt and water, and it keeps for weeks in a sealed tub.

activities.title: Crayon rubbings of hidden shapes
activities.oneLiner: What shape is sleeping under the paper?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, a chunky crayon with the wrapper peeled, flat textured things.
activities.getReady: Find a few flat shapes like a coin, a leaf or a tile.
activities.howToDoIt: Lay paper over a shape and rub the crayon flat until it appears.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose what to hide and reveal next.
activities.trySaying: "You made that appear all on your own."
activities.ifNotWorking: Hold the paper steady while they do the rubbing.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child rubs one big shape with your hand nearby.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds a whole picture from different rubbings.
activities.builds: Doing the whole job themselves, start to finish.
activities.whyItWorks: A shape appearing from nowhere feels like real magic they made.
activities.downTheTrack: Believing you can make things happen is the root of having a go at anything.
activities.safety: Rubbing with the side of the crayon works far better than the tip.

activities.title: Real circle or not?
activities.oneLiner: Is a plate a circle? Is a pillow?
activities.whatYouNeed: A pile of household objects, two spots on the floor.
activities.getReady: Gather round things and nearly-round things together.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort each object into circle or not-a-circle, and talk about the close ones.
activities.howToGuide: Ask why, do not correct them straight away.
activities.trySaying: "It looks round, but is it really?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Trace the edge with a finger to feel for corners.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts clear circles from clear squares.
activities.makeHarder: An older one explains what makes a circle a circle.
activities.builds: Weighing up something that almost fits before deciding.
activities.whyItWorks: The tricky in-between objects are where real thinking happens.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling close-enough from truly right matters more as answers come easy and fast.
activities.safety: Keep buttons and small round counters away from under-threes and out of mouths, as they are a choking hazard.

activities.title: Shape people with your bodies
activities.oneLiner: Can two of us make a triangle on the floor?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear bit of floor and your bodies.
activities.getReady: Push any furniture out of the way first.
activities.howToDoIt: Work together to make shapes with arms, legs and whole bodies.
activities.howToGuide: Let them boss the plan and you follow their lead.
activities.trySaying: "What if we both curl up for a circle?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with a straight line before trying a corner.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child makes a shape with just their arms.
activities.makeHarder: An older one directs the whole family into one big shape.
activities.builds: Reading each other and keeping at it until the shape holds.
activities.whyItWorks: You need two people cooperating, so a triangle takes real teamwork.
activities.downTheTrack: Working well with other people is the skill machines cannot copy.
activities.safety: A soft rug saves knees and elbows during the wobbly bits.

activities.title: Cut and stick a shape picture
activities.oneLiner: What can you build from just squares and triangles?
activities.whatYouNeed: Old paper or magazines, glue, a base sheet, scissors.
activities.getReady: Cut a stack of shapes yourself before you start.
activities.howToDoIt: Arrange the shapes into a house, a boat or a face, then glue them down.
activities.howToGuide: Wait through the fiddly gluing without jumping in.
activities.trySaying: "What will your triangle turn into?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Lay the whole picture out dry before any glue comes near.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sticks two shapes into anything they like.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plans the picture first, then finds the shapes for it.
activities.builds: Seeing a plan through the slow, sticky, frustrating middle.
activities.whyItWorks: Shapes become whatever they imagine, so they own the whole idea.
activities.downTheTrack: Finishing something hard, not just starting it, is what sets people apart.
activities.safety: An adult does the scissors, and small cut pieces stay away from under-threes and out of mouths.

themes.bringItTogether: Shapes are everywhere once you start looking, so keep spotting, building and making them together long after this menu runs out.

themes.title: Numbers all around
themes.hook: Count the real world, not flashcards.

activities.title: Counting walk
activities.oneLiner: How many red cars will we pass?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just a walk out the front door.
activities.getReady: Pick one thing to count before you leave, like dogs or letterboxes.
activities.howToDoIt: Count out loud together every time you spot one.
activities.howToGuide: Let them lose count and start again without a fuss.
activities.trySaying: "That's four now, what comes next?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Count something that turns up often, like fence posts.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child counts to five with your finger pointing along.
activities.makeHarder: An older one keeps a running total the whole way home.
activities.builds: Holding a number in their head while the world keeps moving.
activities.whyItWorks: The count lives in the real street, not on a card.
activities.downTheTrack: Paying steady attention in a busy world is getting rarer and more valuable.
activities.safety: Counting real moving things is much harder than counting still ones, so go gently.

activities.title: Set the table for everyone
activities.oneLiner: How many forks do we need tonight?
activities.whatYouNeed: Plates, cutlery and the people eating.
activities.getReady: Count the chairs together before you start.
activities.howToDoIt: Work out how many of each thing and lay a place for every person.
activities.howToGuide: Let them fetch the wrong number and sort it out themselves.
activities.trySaying: "One for each of us, so how many is that?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Do one place setting together first as a model.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child puts one fork by each plate.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds a guest and works out the new total.
activities.builds: Matching a number to real people who are counting on them.
activities.whyItWorks: A missing fork is a problem they can see and fix at once.
activities.downTheTrack: Thinking of other people's needs is quietly at the heart of every good job.
activities.safety: Swap sharp knives for spoons, and let an adult handle anything with a real edge.

activities.title: Guess then count
activities.oneLiner: How many blocks do you reckon are in this jar?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear jar or bowl and a handful of the same small thing.
activities.getReady: Fill the jar with pasta, blocks or gumnuts.
activities.howToDoIt: Everyone guesses first, then tip it out and count to see who was close.
activities.howToGuide: Take their wild guesses seriously, no guess is wrong yet.
activities.trySaying: "Was your guess close, or way off?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use just a few things so the guess feels reachable.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child guesses more or less than their hand.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses, then makes a better second guess halfway through.
