activities.builds: Making a sensible guess, then checking it against what is real.
activities.whyItWorks: The gap between guess and count is where their judgement grows.
activities.downTheTrack: Sizing up a rough answer, then testing it, is how good thinkers stay sharp.
activities.safety: Small counting objects are a choking hazard, so keep them supervised and out of under-threes' mouths.

activities.title: Build a number
activities.oneLiner: Can you show me five without saying it?
activities.whatYouNeed: Stones, buttons, leaves or pasta, and a flat space.
activities.getReady: Gather a small pile of counting bits.
activities.howToDoIt: Make a number look like something, a five-petal flower or a three-legged bug.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide what the number becomes.
activities.trySaying: "You turned four into a whole robot."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start by lining the objects up in a simple row.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child makes any small pile and counts it after.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds a picture where two numbers add together.
activities.builds: Making a number their own instead of just reciting it.
activities.whyItWorks: Five stops being a word and becomes a thing they built.
activities.downTheTrack: Turning a plain idea into something new is creativity no machine owns.
activities.safety: Buttons and small counters stay away from under-threes and out of mouths, as they choke easily.

activities.title: Share it out fairly
activities.oneLiner: How do we split these grapes so it's fair?
activities.whatYouNeed: A snack that comes in bits, like grapes or crackers.
activities.getReady: Wash the fruit and pick who is sharing.
activities.howToDoIt: Hand out one each, round and round, until it is even.
activities.howToGuide: Let them notice an unfair pile before you point it out.
activities.trySaying: "Does everyone have the same, do you think?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Share between just two people first.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child gives one to each person once.
activities.makeHarder: An older one works out what to do with a leftover bit.
activities.builds: Balancing what is fair for everyone at the table.
activities.whyItWorks: Fairness is a real feeling here, not a sum on paper.
activities.downTheTrack: Judging what is fair between people is a call humans will always need to make.
activities.safety: Cut grapes lengthways for little ones, as whole grapes are a serious choking risk.

activities.title: The big count challenge
activities.oneLiner: Can we count all the way to fifty steps?
activities.whatYouNeed: Your feet, or a big pile of pebbles.
activities.getReady: Pick a big number that feels like a stretch.
activities.howToDoIt: Count steps, pebbles or claps all the way there without stopping.
activities.howToGuide: Cheer them past the tricky spots instead of taking over the count.
activities.trySaying: "We're nearly there, keep going."
activities.ifNotWorking: Break it into chunks of ten and rest between.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child aims for ten with you counting alongside.
activities.makeHarder: An older one counts in twos or backwards from the top.
activities.builds: Pushing through a long job when it gets boring or tricky.
activities.whyItWorks: Reaching fifty feels like a real win they earned step by step.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking at something dull until it is done is a strength that never goes out of date.
activities.safety: Most little kids trip up in the teens, so thirteen to nineteen is the hard bit.

themes.bringItTogether: Numbers are hiding in the walk, the table and the snack bowl, so keep counting the real world together and leave the flashcards on the shelf.

themes.title: Patterns
themes.hook: Spot a pattern hiding in the world, then make one all your own.

activities.title: Clap it back
activities.oneLiner: Can you copy my beat, then sneak in a new one?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just your hands and voices.
activities.getReady: Sit facing each other with a bit of room.
activities.howToDoIt: Clap a short pattern like clap-clap-pause. They copy it back. Then swap and they lead.
activities.howToGuide: Watch their face and wait. Let them be the leader as often as you are.
activities.trySaying: "Now you make one up and I'll copy you."
activities.ifNotWorking: Slow right down to two claps. Add a big smile.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children copy one clap at a time.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds stamps and knee-pats into a three-part beat.
activities.builds: Holding your focus on someone else and matching them beat for beat.
activities.whyItWorks: A pattern you can hear trains the ear before the eye ever gets involved.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading other people closely, a human skill no machine will hand back to us.
activities.safety: Copying a rhythm is early maths and early music, both at once.

activities.title: Backyard pattern hunt
activities.oneLiner: What repeats out here if you really look?
activities.whatYouNeed: Your eyes and a slow walk.
activities.getReady: Head outside and agree to go quietly and look hard.
activities.howToDoIt: Hunt for things that repeat. Bricks in a row, stripes on a leaf, pickets on a fence, ripples in a puddle.
activities.howToGuide: Follow where they point. Ask before you explain.
activities.trySaying: "What can you find that goes again and again?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Point out one clear pattern to start the hunt, then step back.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children spot one repeating thing and that is plenty.
activities.makeHarder: An older one works out the rule, like brick then gap then brick.
activities.builds: Noticing the hidden order in ordinary things nobody points out.
activities.whyItWorks: Looking for a rule turns a plain yard into a puzzle worth walking slowly through.
activities.downTheTrack: Spotting the pattern underneath the mess, which is most of what clear thinking is.
activities.safety: Patterns in nature are real and everywhere, from spider webs to the segments on a slater.

activities.title: Threaded pasta strings
activities.oneLiner: Can you make a rule and keep it going?
activities.whatYouNeed: Dry penne or tube pasta, a shoelace or string with a taped end.
activities.getReady: Tie a big knot at one end so nothing slides off. Sit at the table.
activities.howToDoIt: Thread the pasta in a pattern they choose, like two long then one short, over and over.
activities.howToGuide: Let their fingers do the fiddly work even when it takes a while.
activities.trySaying: "What comes next in your rule?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use bigger tubes and thread onto a chopstick first.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children just thread, no rule needed yet.
activities.makeHarder: An older one paints the pasta two colours first and patterns by colour.
activities.builds: Making a rule with your own hands and holding it steady to the end.
activities.whyItWorks: The string will not lie, so a broken pattern is easy to see and fix.
activities.downTheTrack: Finishing fiddly work you started, when the easy thing is to give up halfway.
activities.safety: Keep pasta out of mouths and well away from any child under three, it is a choking risk. Stay at the table the whole time.

activities.title: Set the table your way
activities.oneLiner: Can you lay each place so they all match?
activities.whatYouNeed: Plates, cups and spoons for the family.
activities.getReady: Stack everything within easy reach on the bench.
activities.howToDoIt: They set each place the same way. Plate, then cup on the right, then spoon on top, matching every seat.
activities.howToGuide: Let them carry and place. Resist tidying it to your liking.
activities.trySaying: "Does every spot look the same as the last one?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Do one place setting together as the model, then hand it over.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children just put one spoon at each seat.
activities.makeHarder: An older one folds a napkin into each spot too.
activities.builds: Doing a real family job and getting every place to match.
activities.whyItWorks: A laid table is a pattern the whole family sits down inside.
activities.downTheTrack: Believing your own two hands can get a real job done properly.
activities.safety: Use plastic or melamine, not glass or sharp knives, near little hands.

activities.title: Spot the wrong one
activities.oneLiner: Which one snuck in and broke the rule?
activities.whatYouNeed: Blocks, socks or spoons, anything you have a few of.
activities.getReady: Lay out a simple repeating line while they watch.
activities.howToDoIt: Make a pattern, then sneak in one that breaks it. They hunt down the odd one and fix it.
activities.howToGuide: Give them time to find it before you say a word.
activities.trySaying: "Something in here doesn't belong. Can you find it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the odd one very obvious, like a big red block in a blue line.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children point to the one that looks different.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds the tricky pattern for you to check.
activities.builds: Telling the sensible from the silly by checking against a rule.
activities.whyItWorks: Hunting the odd one out makes them look twice instead of once.
activities.downTheTrack: Catching the thing that is off when everything else looks fine, which keeps us safe.
activities.safety: Finding the thing that does not fit is the start of good judgement.

activities.title: Invent a moving pattern
activities.oneLiner: Can you build a dance from three moves?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear space and some music if you like.
activities.getReady: Push back chairs and clear the floor so nobody trips.
activities.howToDoIt: Pick three moves, like jump, spin, stamp. Put them in an order and repeat it as a dance.
activities.howToGuide: Let them choose the moves and the order, even the odd ones.
activities.trySaying: "Show me your pattern again, exactly the same."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with just two moves and do it slowly together.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children repeat one move over and over.
activities.makeHarder: An older one teaches their dance to you and checks you get it right.
activities.builds: Making up something new and keeping it going the same each time.
activities.whyItWorks: A pattern you dance lives in the body, not just the head.
activities.downTheTrack: Inventing your own way to do a thing, then having the patience to nail it.
activities.safety: Clear the space of hard corners and rugs before any jumping.

themes.bringItTogether: Patterns are the world whispering its rules, and once your child can hear them, copy them and make their own, they carry a quiet superpower into everything from music to maths to reading people.

themes.title: Make a story
themes.hook: Invent one together, then act it out with your whole bodies.

activities.title: Meet the sock
activities.oneLiner: Who lives inside this old sock?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clean odd sock for each of you.
activities.getReady: Fish two lonely socks out of the drawer.
activities.howToDoIt: Slip a sock on your hand and give it a name, a voice and one big feeling. Let the two socks meet and talk.
activities.howToGuide: Ask their sock questions and really listen to the answers.
activities.trySaying: "What's your sock's name, and what does it love?"
activities.ifNotWorking: You go first and let your sock be a bit silly to break the ice.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children just wave the sock and make a noise.
activities.makeHarder: An older one gives the sock a worry and a wish.
activities.builds: Imagining a whole person out of nothing and caring what happens to them.
activities.whyItWorks: A voice on your hand is easier to be brave with than your own.
activities.downTheTrack: Understanding how another mind feels, which is the heart of getting on with people.
activities.safety: Giving a character a feeling is the first thread of every story.

activities.title: What happens next walk
activities.oneLiner: Where does the story go from here?
activities.whatYouNeed: Nothing but a wander.
activities.getReady: Pick a starting line together, like "One day a small dog found a door."
activities.howToDoIt: Walk slowly and take turns adding what happens next, one bit each, as you go.
activities.howToGuide: Take their wild ideas and build on them, do not tidy them up.
activities.trySaying: "And then what happened?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Offer two choices, like "does the door open or does it wobble?"
activities.makeEasier: Younger children point at things and you weave them in.
activities.makeHarder: An older one has to link back to something from earlier in the tale.
activities.builds: Asking what if and following the idea wherever it runs.
activities.whyItWorks: Walking loosens the mind, so the next idea arrives on its own.
activities.downTheTrack: Dreaming up what could happen next, the move a machine cannot make for you.
activities.safety: Stories made up out loud stretch language faster than most books do.

activities.title: Act the brave bit
activities.oneLiner: Can you show me the scary part with your body?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear space and maybe a cushion or two.
activities.getReady: Move furniture back so there is room to move safely.
activities.howToDoIt: Pick the exciting part of your story, like crossing a wobbly bridge, and act it out big with tiptoes and freezes.
activities.howToGuide: Let the child steer how scary it gets and when it stops.
activities.trySaying: "You're the boss of this bit. How brave do we go?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make it smaller and gentler, or let a sock character be brave instead.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children do one big action, like a giant stomp.
activities.makeHarder: An older one acts a problem and how the hero gets out of it.
activities.builds: Facing a pretend scary moment and choosing to keep going.
activities.whyItWorks: Trying on brave in a story lets them practise it where it is safe.
activities.downTheTrack: Backing yourself to act when things feel hard or uncertain.
activities.safety: Clear the floor of hard edges and rugs, and stop the moment they want to stop.

activities.title: Make the sounds
activities.oneLiner: What does your story sound like?
activities.whatYouNeed: Household bits, like a wooden spoon, a cup of rice, crinkly paper.
activities.getReady: Gather a few noise-makers on the floor between you.
activities.howToDoIt: Tell the story again while they add the sounds. Tap for footsteps, shake rice for rain, crackle paper for fire.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide which object makes which sound.
activities.trySaying: "What could rain sound like in our story?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Do one sound together first, like knuckles knocking for a door.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children make the sounds with their mouth and hands.
activities.makeHarder: An older one cues each sound at exactly the right moment.
activities.builds: Matching a real object to the job you need it to do.
activities.whyItWorks: Listening for the right moment keeps their focus glued to the tale.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing exactly the right instant to act, which is half of doing anything well.
activities.safety: Keep loose rice sealed in a cup or bag and away from any child under three, it is a choking risk.

activities.title: How does everyone feel
activities.oneLiner: What's going on inside each character?
activities.whatYouNeed: Your story and your faces.
activities.getReady: Pause the story at a moment where something happens.
activities.howToDoIt: Stop and ask how each character feels right now, and pull the face to match. Happy, cross, worried, proud.
activities.howToGuide: Take every answer seriously, even if the wolf feels shy.
activities.trySaying: "How do you think she feels right now?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Offer two feelings and let them pick and pull the face.
activities.makeEasier: Younger children just show happy or sad.
activities.makeHarder: An older one explains why the character feels that way.
activities.builds: Reading what someone else feels and caring about the answer.
activities.whyItWorks: A story is a safe place to try on feelings that are not yours.
activities.downTheTrack: Telling how people really feel under the surface, which no screen can do for you.
activities.safety: Naming feelings out loud is how children learn to handle their own.

activities.title: Could this really happen
activities.oneLiner: Is this bit real or is it pretend?
activities.whatYouNeed: Your finished story.
activities.getReady: Sit together and think back over the whole tale.
activities.howToDoIt: Go through the parts and sort them. A dog that barks is real. A dog that flies is pretend. Talk about which is which.
activities.howToGuide: Ask them to explain their reason, do not just correct.
activities.trySaying: "Could that really happen, or only in a story?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with easy ones, like "can a cat drive a car?"
activities.makeEasier: Younger children give a thumbs up for real and down for pretend.
activities.makeHarder: An older one changes a pretend bit into something that could really happen.
activities.builds: Telling what is real from what is invented, and enjoying each for what it is.
activities.whyItWorks: Their own story is the gentlest place to practise a sharp question.
activities.downTheTrack: Knowing real from fake, the skill that matters most as screens blur the line.
activities.safety: Sorting real from make-believe is a big thinking step at this age, and it is fine to love both.

themes.bringItTogether: When your child invents a story and acts it out, they are rehearsing being human, feeling with others, being brave, and telling what is real, all wrapped up in play they will beg to do again.

themes.title: Big Feelings
themes.subtitle: name them, show them, sit with them
themes.hook: Feelings are big and loud in little bodies, and none of them are bad. Your job is not to fix the storm but to sit close while it passes. When a child feels heard, the feeling gets smaller on its own.

activities.title: The feelings weather report
activities.oneLiner: Is it sunny inside today, or a bit stormy?
activities.place: Anywhere, morning or after a wobble
activities.whatYouNeed: Just the two of you. A window helps.
activities.getReady: Pick a quiet moment, not the middle of a meltdown.
activities.howToDoIt: Ask what the weather is like inside their body today. Sunny, cloudy, windy, or a big thunderstorm.
activities.howToGuide: Give your own report first, then wait. Let them borrow your words if they want them.
activities.trySaying: "I'm a bit cloudy this morning. How about you?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Point at the real sky and start there, then come back inside.
activities.makeEasier: Offer two choices, sunny or stormy, and let them point.
activities.makeHarder: Ask what might turn a storm back to sunshine by lunchtime.
activities.builds: Noticing what is going on inside before it spills out.
activities.whyItWorks: Weather words give a shape to feelings that are too big to say plainly.
activities.downTheTrack: Knowing your own inner state is the skill no machine can do for you.
activities.safety: Naming a feeling out loud helps settle the part of the brain that is racing.

activities.title: Feelings detective
activities.oneLiner: Can you guess how they feel just by looking?
activities.whatYouNeed: A picture book with faces, or old photos.
activities.getReady: Find a few pages with clear expressions, happy, cross, scared, surprised.
activities.howToDoIt: Look at a face together and work out what that person might be feeling and why.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder out loud, do not correct. There is often more than one right answer.
activities.trySaying: "Look at her eyebrows. What do you reckon happened just before this?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Pull the face yourself and let them read you instead.
activities.makeEasier: Stick to happy and sad, the two easiest to spot.
activities.makeHarder: Try the tricky ones like worried, jealous, or proud.
activities.builds: Caring enough to wonder what someone else is feeling.
activities.whyItWorks: A still face is a puzzle, and telling worried from cross takes real judgement.
activities.downTheTrack: Reading people well is what makes a good friend, teammate and leader.
activities.safety: Reading faces is a learned skill, and some kids need lots of practice. That is normal.

activities.title: Build a calm corner
activities.oneLiner: Where could you go when everything feels too much?
activities.whatYouNeed: Cushions, a blanket, a soft toy, a favourite book.
activities.getReady: Find a corner that is out of the way and a bit tucked in.
activities.howToDoIt: Let the child design their own cosy spot for when feelings get big. They choose what goes in it.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their plan even if it looks odd to you. It is theirs.
activities.trySaying: "This is your spot. What would make it feel safe?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Build it together over a few days instead of all at once.
activities.makeEasier: Drape a blanket over two chairs and pop a cushion inside.
activities.makeHarder: Ask them to draw a little sign or a rule for the corner.
activities.builds: Knowing you can do something helpful when a feeling gets loud.
activities.whyItWorks: Choosing their own tools tells a child their feelings are worth minding.
activities.downTheTrack: Managing your own state under pressure is a lifelong steadying skill.
activities.safety: A calm corner is a soft choice, never a punishment or a time-out spot.

activities.title: Breathe with a bear
activities.oneLiner: Can you rock your teddy to sleep with your breath?
activities.whatYouNeed: A soft toy that sits on the tummy.
activities.getReady: Lie down somewhere comfy, on backs.
activities.howToDoIt: Rest the toy on the belly and watch it ride up and down with slow breaths.
activities.howToGuide: Slow your own breath right down. They will drift towards your pace.
activities.trySaying: "Let's give Bear a gentle ride, up slow and down slow."
activities.ifNotWorking: Just lie together and rest. The calm still counts.
activities.makeEasier: Count one up, one down, nice and short.
activities.makeHarder: See if they can keep it slow for ten rides in a row.
activities.builds: Staying with something quiet even when part of you wants to jump up.
activities.whyItWorks: A toy that moves turns invisible breathing into something a child can see and steer.
activities.downTheTrack: Being able to settle yourself is a quiet strength that carries a whole life.
activities.safety: Slow belly breathing really does calm the body, and it is gentle. Never hold the breath or force it.

activities.title: Where do you feel it?
activities.oneLiner: When you're cross, where does it live in your body?
activities.whatYouNeed: Big paper, crayons.
activities.getReady: Draw a rough gingerbread body outline together, or trace their hand.
activities.howToDoIt: Talk about where different feelings sit. Butterflies in the tummy, hot cheeks when cross, a lump in the throat when sad. Colour those spots in.
activities.howToGuide: Ask questions instead of giving answers. They are the expert on their own body.
activities.trySaying: "When you feel scared, where does it go? Show me."
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with a happy feeling, that one is easier to find.
activities.makeEasier: You colour while they point and tell you where.
activities.makeHarder: Add what helps each spot feel better again.
activities.builds: Caring curiosity about what is happening inside.
activities.whyItWorks: Asking where a feeling lives turns a vague upset into something a child can point to.
activities.downTheTrack: Tuning in to your own signals early keeps small stresses from becoming big ones.
activities.safety: Feelings really do show up in the body, and noticing that is a healthy first step, not therapy.

activities.title: Scribble the big one out
activities.oneLiner: How big is that feeling? Show me on the paper.
activities.whatYouNeed: Butcher's paper or the back of old wrapping, fat crayons.
activities.getReady: Tape the paper down so it will not slide.
activities.howToDoIt: When a feeling is big, let them draw it. Fast scribbles for cross, slow swirls for sad, whatever comes.
activities.howToGuide: No drawing lessons here. Let the hand move however the feeling wants.
activities.trySaying: "Make the paper show me how big it feels."
activities.ifNotWorking: Sit beside them and scribble your own feeling first.
activities.makeEasier: One colour, big arm movements, no plan.
activities.makeHarder: Ask them to tell you the story the scribble is holding.
activities.builds: Caring space for a feeling to come out safely.
activities.whyItWorks: A big feeling needs somewhere to go, and paper takes it without anyone getting hurt.
activities.downTheTrack: Turning feelings into something you can look at is how creative, steady people cope.
activities.safety: All feelings are allowed, even the loud ones. If a child is truly distressed, put the crayons down and comfort first.

themes.bringItTogether: Feelings are visitors, not the boss. When you name them, show them and sit with them, your child learns the storm always passes and they are never alone in it.

themes.title: The Pretend Shop
themes.subtitle: serve, choose, swap, role-play the grown-up world
themes.hook: A cardboard box becomes a corner store, a bottle top becomes a coin, and your child becomes the grown-up in charge. Pretend shops are where kids practise the whole big world in miniature, from counting out change to saying "next please" with a smile.

activities.title: Open for business
activities.oneLiner: What kind of shop should we run today?
activities.whatYouNeed: A box or low table, empty clean packets and tins, a tea towel.
activities.getReady: Save a few clean, safe empties from the recycling.
activities.howToDoIt: Let the child decide the shop, a fruit shop, a cafe, a servo. Set out the goods and open up.
activities.howToGuide: Let them run it. You be the first customer and follow their lead.
activities.trySaying: "You're the boss. What are you selling today?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with three items only, less to sort out.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just lines things up and hands them over.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes a sign and sorts goods into sections.
activities.builds: Setting something real up from scratch, with your own hands.
activities.whyItWorks: Running a shop means solving a dozen little real world problems in a row.
activities.downTheTrack: Getting an idea off the ground yourself is the skill behind every job that lasts.
activities.safety: Check every tin has no sharp lid, and keep small empties like bottle caps out of little mouths.

activities.title: Make the money
activities.oneLiner: Every shop needs coins. Can we make our own?
activities.whatYouNeed: Milk bottle lids or jar lids, cardboard, a marker.
activities.getReady: Cut a few cardboard circles bigger than a fifty cent piece.
activities.howToDoIt: Make pretend coins and notes together. Draw numbers or dots on them and decide what each is worth.
activities.howToGuide: Let their money make sense to them, even if a leaf is worth ten dollars.
activities.trySaying: "How much should this shiny one be worth?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use real leaves or gumnuts as coins instead, no cutting needed.
activities.makeEasier: Skip the numbers, just make lots of the same coin.
activities.makeHarder: Make coins of different values and practise swapping five ones for a five.
activities.builds: Making a brand new thing that the whole game then runs on.
activities.whyItWorks: Inventing money means deciding what stands for what, which is real thinking dressed up as play.
activities.downTheTrack: Comfort with making things up and giving them value sits behind design and invention.
activities.safety: Keep every pretend coin bigger than a toilet roll tube so it cannot be swallowed, and no coins in mouths.

activities.title: Next please
activities.oneLiner: Can you serve me like a real shopkeeper?
activities.whatYouNeed: The shop, the coins, a pretend phone or bag.
activities.getReady: Nothing extra, just step into character.
activities.howToDoIt: Take turns being shopkeeper and customer. Say hello, ask what they need, wrap it up, say thanks.
activities.howToGuide: Play a customer with a little feeling, tired, cheerful, in a rush, and see how they respond.
activities.trySaying: "Good morning, do you have any bananas today?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop the words and just pass goods back and forth with a smile.
activities.makeEasier: You lead every line and they copy it back.
activities.makeHarder: Be a customer who cannot decide, and let them help you choose.
activities.builds: Reading a customer and caring how they are treated.
activities.whyItWorks: Pretending to be the grown-up lets a child try on manners and kindness with no pressure.
activities.downTheTrack: Warmth and good service between people is exactly what machines cannot fake.
activities.safety: Role-play like this is how kids practise the polite back-and-forth of real life.

activities.title: Sort the shelves
activities.oneLiner: Where does everything belong?
activities.whatYouNeed: The shop goods, a few boxes or trays.
activities.getReady: Muddle all the goods into one pile.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort the stock onto shelves. All the food here, drinks there, the cold things together.
activities.howToGuide: Let them pick the sorting rule. Ask why they put things where they did.
activities.trySaying: "Which things go together, do you think?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Sort by one thing only, like big and little.
activities.makeEasier: Two groups is plenty for a younger child.
activities.makeHarder: Add price tags and put the cheap things on one shelf.
activities.builds: Holding focus while everything finds its right spot.
activities.whyItWorks: Deciding what belongs with what is judgement, telling the sensible group from the silly one.
activities.downTheTrack: Sorting signal from noise is the thinking that keeps you sharp in a world full of information.
activities.safety: Sorting is early maths, and there is often more than one sensible way to do it.

activities.title: The great swap
activities.oneLiner: No coins today. What will you trade?
activities.place: The pretend shop or the yard
activities.whatYouNeed: Two small piles of goods or nature bits, one each.
activities.getReady: Share the goods out so you both have things to trade.
activities.howToDoIt: Swap items with no money. Is two pinecones a fair trade for one gumnut? Talk it through.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder about fairness out loud. Let them push back and haggle.
activities.trySaying: "Hmm, is that a fair swap? What do you reckon?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start by swapping one thing for one thing, dead even.
activities.makeEasier: Trade identical items so fairness is obvious.
activities.makeHarder: Give some items more value and see if they spot a dud deal.
activities.builds: Asking whether a deal makes sense before saying yes.
activities.whyItWorks: Working out a fair swap is real judgement, telling a good offer from a rip-off.
activities.downTheTrack: Weighing what something is really worth keeps you hard to fool.
activities.safety: Bartering is how people traded long before coins, a nice true fact to share.

activities.title: Sold out and sorry
activities.oneLiner: Oh no, we've run out. What now?
activities.whatYouNeed: The shop, set up as normal.
activities.getReady: Quietly hide one popular item before you start.
activities.howToDoIt: As customer, ask for the missing thing. Let the shopkeeper handle the hiccup, apologise, offer something else, or promise it tomorrow.
activities.howToGuide: Do not rescue them straight away. Let them sit in the tricky bit and find a way through.
activities.trySaying: "Oh, you're out of milk? That's alright, what else have you got?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Turn it into restocking the shelf together instead.
activities.makeEasier: Have the missing item reappear quickly so the wobble is small.
activities.makeHarder: Throw in a customer who is a bit grumpy about it.
activities.builds: Staying steady when the plan hits a snag.
activities.whyItWorks: A sold-out shop is a gentle problem, and smoothing it over means minding the customer's feelings too.
activities.downTheTrack: Rolling with a setback and keeping people onside is what carries you through any changing job.
activities.safety: Handling a small letdown in play builds patience for the real ones.

themes.bringItTogether: In the pretend shop your child gets to be the capable grown-up, counting, choosing, serving and coping when things go sideways. Every swap and every "next please" is the wide world practised small.

themes.title: Space
themes.subtitle: the moon, the sun, the stars, and blasting off
themes.hook: Wonder is the whole point up here. We look close, we guess what will happen, then we find out together.

activities.title: Moon watcher's diary
activities.oneLiner: What shape is the moon tonight?
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, a pencil, a spot where you can see the sky.
activities.getReady: Fold one sheet into little boxes, one box for each night.
activities.howToDoIt: Look for the moon after dark and draw the shape you see in tonight's box.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide what shape it is, even if it looks wonky.
activities.trySaying: "Is it round tonight, or a slice?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Cloudy nights happen. Leave the box empty and try tomorrow.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just points and you draw it.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses tomorrow's shape before bed.
activities.builds: Noticing one small thing change, night after night.
activities.whyItWorks: Guessing the next shape is a real prediction they can check.
activities.downTheTrack: Spotting slow patterns over time is how good thinking beats a quick guess.
activities.safety: The moon slowly changes shape over about a month, then starts again. It makes no light of its own. It only glows because the sun shines on it.

activities.title: Chase your shadow
activities.oneLiner: Can your shadow shrink and stretch?
activities.whatYouNeed: Chalk or a few small stones, a sunny bit of concrete or dirt.
activities.getReady: Find an open spot with room to stand still.
activities.howToDoIt: Trace or mark where their shadow lands, then come back a couple of hours later and mark it again.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what they think will happen before you check the second time.
activities.trySaying: "Where do you reckon your shadow will be later?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a bottle or a toy as the shadow-maker so nobody has to hold still.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child stomps on your shadow instead of tracing.
activities.makeHarder: An older one predicts if the shadow will be longer or shorter by afternoon.
activities.builds: A guess made first, then tested against what really happened.
activities.whyItWorks: The sun moves across the sky through the day, so the shadow shifts too, and they see it for themselves.
activities.downTheTrack: Guess, then check is the heart of every real experiment and every honest answer.
activities.safety: Never look straight at the sun. Watch the ground and the shadow, not the sky.

activities.title: Wonder at the stars
activities.oneLiner: How many stars can two people count?
activities.whatYouNeed: A rug or towel, a clear-ish night, each other.
activities.getReady: Clear any trip hazards on the way out to your spot before dark.
activities.howToDoIt: Lie back together, let your eyes settle, and share the stars you find.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder out loud with them instead of naming things for them.
activities.trySaying: "I wonder what those stars are made of."
activities.ifNotWorking: City lights hide stars. Try the brightest one, or the moon, and talk about that.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child spots just one star and names it something silly.
activities.makeHarder: An older one makes up a picture from a group of stars.
activities.builds: Sharing quiet wonder with someone you love.
activities.whyItWorks: Big questions with no quick answer keep curiosity alive.
activities.downTheTrack: Wondering together, not alone, is where the best questions come from.
activities.safety: Stars are giant balls of hot, glowing gas, a bit like our sun, but so far away they look tiny.

activities.title: Junk-box rocket
activities.oneLiner: Can you build a rocket that stands up on its own?
activities.whatYouNeed: An empty bottle or tube, paper, sticky tape, bottle lids, textas.
activities.getReady: Put the bits in a pile and let them pick.
activities.howToDoIt: Build a rocket that can stand on the table without falling.
activities.howToGuide: When it topples, wait. Let them work out why before you jump in.
activities.trySaying: "What could make the bottom more steady?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with the wide bottle as the base and add from there.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child tapes on lids and calls it done.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds fins and a pointy nose that stay put.
activities.builds: Making a real thing with your own hands and choices.
activities.whyItWorks: A rocket that keeps toppling is a problem with many possible fixes.
activities.downTheTrack: Being the one who builds and decides, not just watches, is a strength no machine takes from you.
activities.safety: Real rockets are pointy at the top so they slip through the air more easily.

activities.title: Make a moon crater
activities.oneLiner: What happens when a rock hits the moon?
activities.whatYouNeed: A tray, plain flour, a spoon of cocoa or cinnamon, small stones or marbles.
activities.getReady: Fill the tray with flour and dust the top so it goes darker.
activities.howToDoIt: Drop stones from up high and look at the dents they leave.
activities.howToGuide: Ask them to guess if a big stone or a little one makes a bigger hole, then drop both.
activities.trySaying: "Big rock or small rock, which makes the bigger dent?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop from higher up for a clearer crater, and smooth the flour between goes.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just plops stones in and pokes the holes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one drops from low then high and compares the dents.
activities.builds: Testing a guess by actually doing it, not just wondering.
activities.whyItWorks: The moon's craters really were made by rocks crashing into it, and here they can see how a dent forms.
activities.downTheTrack: Trusting a test over a hunch is how you tell what is true from what only sounds true.
activities.safety: Supervise the flour so it stays in the tray, and wash hands after. Drop stones, never throw them.

activities.title: Ten, nine, blast off
activities.oneLiner: Can you power a rocket with just air?
activities.whatYouNeed: A balloon, a straw, string, sticky tape, two chairs.
activities.getReady: Thread the string through the straw and tie it tight between two chairs.
activities.howToDoIt: Tape a blown-up balloon to the straw, hold the neck, count down, then let go and watch it shoot along.
activities.howToGuide: Let them do the blowing, holding and releasing, even when it takes a few tries.
activities.trySaying: "Ready? Ten, nine, eight, blast off!"
activities.ifNotWorking: Pull the string tighter and check the straw slides freely first.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just lets go while you hold the balloon.
activities.makeHarder: An older one tries a fatter balloon and guesses if it goes further.
activities.builds: Doing every step yourself and owning the launch.
activities.whyItWorks: Blowing up and re-taping again and again grows patience through the wobbles.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with something fiddly until it flies is grit you carry into any hard job.
activities.safety: The air rushing out the back pushes the balloon forward. A real rocket pushes itself up the same way.

themes.bringItTogether: Across these six you looked closely, guessed and checked, built with your hands and wondered side by side, which is exactly what real science feels like at this age.

themes.title: Living things
themes.subtitle: what is alive, what isn't, and how we can tell
themes.hook: Alive is a puzzle worth poking at. We look, we guess, we check, and we treat every little creature gently.

activities.title: Alive or not?
activities.oneLiner: Is a rock alive? How can we tell?
activities.whatYouNeed: A basket, and a few things like a leaf, a stone, a toy, a stick, a flower.
activities.getReady: Collect five or six bits and pop them on the floor.
activities.howToDoIt: Sort them into a pile for alive or once-alive and a pile for never-alive.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide, then ask how they knew. A leaf being tricky is good.
activities.trySaying: "Does it grow? Does it need a drink?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with two easy ones, a pet toy and a real pet plant.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child sorts just two things, alive and not.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds a fallen leaf and works out the once-alive pile.
activities.builds: Judging a tricky case by asking the right questions.
activities.whyItWorks: The wobbly ones, like a leaf or a stick, have no single easy answer.
activities.downTheTrack: Sorting true from tricky by testing your own reasons is clear thinking for life.
activities.safety: Living things grow, need food or water, and make more of themselves. A picked leaf was alive but is not any more.

activities.title: Feel the thump
activities.oneLiner: Can you find the drum inside your chest?
activities.whatYouNeed: Just the two of you and a quiet spot.
activities.getReady: Sit somewhere calm where you can go still.
activities.howToDoIt: Rest a hand on your chest, feel the thump, then do some star jumps and feel it again.
activities.howToGuide: Let them notice the change themselves instead of telling them.
activities.trySaying: "Can you feel it going faster now?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Feel it on the side of the neck if the chest is hard to find.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just pats along in time with the beat.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses if jumping or resting makes it faster, then checks.
activities.builds: Tuning in to a real signal from your own body.
activities.whyItWorks: Living things do things that non-living things cannot, and a heartbeat is one you can feel.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing what your body and others are telling you is care that stays deeply human.
activities.safety: Your heart beats all day to move blood around your body, and it speeds up when you run. Feeling your own heartbeat is perfectly fine and safe.

activities.title: The waiting seed
activities.oneLiner: Can you wait for a seed to wake up?
activities.time: 10 min a day, over a week
activities.whatYouNeed: A jar, cotton wool or paper towel, a dried bean, water.
activities.getReady: Damp the cotton wool and tuck the bean against the glass so you can see it.
activities.howToDoIt: Keep it just damp and check it each day for a root or a shoot.
activities.howToGuide: Hand them the watering job and let them own it.
activities.trySaying: "Shall we check if anything changed today?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Nothing for days is normal. Keep it damp, not soaked, and keep waiting.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just does the daily water and peek.
activities.makeHarder: An older one draws each day and guesses which end sprouts first.
activities.builds: Patience through slow days with no reward yet.
activities.whyItWorks: A seed answers the big question of what is alive by slowly waking up.
activities.downTheTrack: Caring for something over time, unhurried, is a steadiness screens keep trying to steal.
activities.safety: Wash hands after touching soil or seeds, and never eat the seeds or sprouts.

activities.title: Minibeast safari
activities.oneLiner: Who lives under that log?
activities.whatYouNeed: A magnifying glass if you have one, a soft brush, curious eyes.
activities.getReady: Pick a damp corner of the garden or park.
activities.howToDoIt: Gently lift leaves and logs and see who is home underneath.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder with them about what each little one is doing.
activities.trySaying: "I wonder where it's off to."
activities.ifNotWorking: No bugs about? Try a damper, shadier spot or look under a pot.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just spots and points at movers.
activities.makeHarder: An older one counts the legs and guesses what it eats.
activities.builds: Asking real questions about real lives.
activities.whyItWorks: Live creatures move, feed and hide, showing what alive really means up close.
activities.downTheTrack: Curiosity about the world beyond a screen is where fresh questions are born.
activities.safety: Handle any creature gently and put it straight back where it lived. Wash hands after, and never eat plants or berries.

activities.title: Invent a creature
activities.oneLiner: Can you make an animal nobody has ever seen?
activities.whatYouNeed: Playdough or paper, sticks, leaves, googly eyes or drawn ones.
activities.getReady: Lay out the bits and pieces to choose from.
activities.howToDoIt: Build a made-up creature and decide what it eats and where it lives.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their idea, even a wild one, and keep asking about it.
activities.trySaying: "What does your creature need to stay alive?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start from one real animal and change just one thing about it.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child gives it eyes and a name and stops there.
activities.makeHarder: An older one gives it living-thing needs like food, water and a home.
activities.builds: Making something brand new from your own imagination.
activities.whyItWorks: Deciding what a creature needs uses what they now know about being alive.
activities.downTheTrack: Inventing what does not exist yet is the one thing that stays yours as machines copy the rest.
activities.safety: Every real animal needs food, water and somewhere safe, and a made-up one can too.

activities.title: Snail's slow race
activities.oneLiner: Which way will the snail go?
activities.whatYouNeed: A found snail or slug or worm, a damp leaf, patience.
activities.getReady: Pop the creature gently on a flat, damp surface.
activities.howToDoIt: Guess which way it will head, then watch closely and see if you were right.
activities.howToGuide: Let the guess be theirs and let the waiting be slow.
activities.trySaying: "Left or right? Let's watch and see."
activities.ifNotWorking: A shy snail hides. Wait quietly, or dampen the leaf to tempt it out.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just watches it move and copies the slow crawl.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses if a leaf treat changes its path.
activities.builds: Making a call, then watching patiently to see if it holds.
activities.whyItWorks: A living thing chooses its own way, unlike a rolled stone, and a guess is easy to test.
activities.downTheTrack: Watching closely before deciding you are right keeps you honest when answers come fast.
activities.safety: Hold it gently, keep it damp, and put it back exactly where you found it. Wash hands after.

themes.bringItTogether: These six let a child sort the living from the not, care for small lives gently, wait out a slow seed and invent one of their own, which is how wonder about life takes root.

themes.title: Mixing and changing
themes.hook: Fizz, melt, freeze, and watch stuff transform. Guess what will happen first, then find out together.

activities.title: The kitchen volcano
activities.oneLiner: Can you make it fizz right up over the top?
activities.whatYouNeed: Bicarb soda, white vinegar, a cup, a tray, a teaspoon.
activities.getReady: Stand the cup in the middle of the tray. Put a spoon of bicarb in the cup.
activities.howToDoIt: Pour a little vinegar in and watch it foam. Ask what will happen before each pour.
activities.howToGuide: Let them do the pouring. Wait through the fizz without narrating every second.
activities.trySaying: "Guess first. Big fizz or little fizz?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Add more bicarb, then pour vinegar faster.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just watches you pour and points at the bubbles.
activities.makeHarder: An older one tries to make the biggest fizz by changing the amounts.
activities.builds: Guessing what will happen, then checking it against the real fizz.
activities.whyItWorks: The bubbles are a brand new thing made from two boring powders.
activities.downTheTrack: Testing a hunch instead of just believing it, which machines can't do for you.
activities.safety: Never taste it. Keep it away from eyes and mouths, and wash hands after.

activities.title: Race the melting ice
activities.oneLiner: Which ice cube melts first, and why?
activities.whatYouNeed: A few ice cubes, some small bowls, a warm spot and a cool spot.
activities.getReady: Pop one cube in each bowl. Pick different spots around the room.
activities.howToDoIt: Guess which will melt first, then keep checking back on them.
activities.howToGuide: Ask where the warm places are. Let them move a cube if they want to.
activities.trySaying: "Which one do you reckon will win?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Put one cube in your hand and one on the bench so the race is quick.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child holds one cube and feels it turn to water.
activities.makeHarder: An older one wraps a cube in a tea towel and guesses if that helps.
activities.builds: Close looking at a slow change most people walk straight past.
activities.whyItWorks: A melting cube asks a real question with a real answer you can see.
activities.downTheTrack: Patience to notice slow change, the kind of noticing no app does for you.
activities.safety: Warmth turns solid ice into liquid water. Nothing is lost, it just changes.

activities.title: Make your own ice treasure
activities.oneLiner: Can you freeze something and dig it out tomorrow?
activities.whatYouNeed: A small container, water, a little toy or a leaf, the freezer.
activities.getReady: Drop the toy in the container and fill it with water.
activities.howToDoIt: Put it in the freezer, wait, then work out how to free the toy tomorrow.
activities.howToGuide: Let them decide how to melt it. Warm water, sunshine, or just waiting.
activities.trySaying: "How could we get it out without breaking it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Run the block under the cold tap to loosen the edges.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child freezes plain water and feels how hard it goes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one freezes layers so the toy sits in the middle.
activities.builds: Doing a job that only pays off if you wait for it.
activities.whyItWorks: They set up the change themselves, then come back and finish it.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking with something overnight, when quick answers are everywhere.
activities.safety: An adult handles any warm water. Keep it off little laps.

activities.title: Cornflour goop
activities.oneLiner: Is it a liquid or a solid? Poke it and see.
activities.whatYouNeed: Cornflour, water, a bowl, a spoon, a tray underneath.
activities.getReady: Tip cornflour in the bowl. Add water slowly and mix.
activities.howToDoIt: Get it so it goes hard when you tap it but runny when you rest your hand.
activities.howToGuide: Let them add the water bit by bit and feel it change.
activities.trySaying: "Is it hard or soft? Guess before you poke it."
activities.ifNotWorking: Too runny needs more cornflour. Too stiff needs a splash of water.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just squishes it and lets it drip.
activities.makeHarder: An older one rolls a ball fast, then watches it melt in their palm.
activities.builds: Working the mix with your hands until it does the strange thing.
activities.whyItWorks: There is no one right recipe, so they invent their own feel for it.
activities.downTheTrack: Trusting your own test over what you were told to expect.
activities.safety: Never taste it. Keep it out of eyes, and wash hands after.

activities.title: Where did the colour go
activities.oneLiner: Watch a drop of colour spread through the water.
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear glass of water, food colouring or cordial, a spoon.
activities.getReady: Fill the glass and set it somewhere still.
activities.howToDoIt: Drop one drop in and watch the colour swirl and spread without stirring.
activities.howToGuide: Sit close and watch together. Wonder out loud about the swirls.
activities.trySaying: "Where do you think the colour is going?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Warmer water makes the colour move quicker and clearer.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child drops the colour and stirs it into one shade.
activities.makeHarder: An older one drops two colours and guesses what mix they will make.
activities.builds: Sitting still and noticing a slow, quiet change side by side.
activities.whyItWorks: Two of you wondering at the same swirl turns a glass into a shared moment.
activities.downTheTrack: Wondering together with someone, a warmth no screen gives back.
activities.safety: The colour spreads on its own as it mixes evenly through the water.

activities.title: The fizzy lifting race
activities.oneLiner: Can bubbles make a raisin dance up and down?
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear glass, soda water or fizzy water, a few sultanas.
activities.getReady: Pour the fizzy water into the glass. Have the sultanas ready.
activities.howToDoIt: Drop sultanas in and watch bubbles carry them up, then drop them back.
activities.howToGuide: Let them add the sultanas and wait. The dance takes a minute to start.
activities.trySaying: "Wait for it. What are the bubbles doing to it?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use fresh fizzy water so there are plenty of bubbles.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just watches the bubbles climb the glass.
activities.makeHarder: An older one counts how many trips a single sultana makes.
activities.builds: Setting it up yourself, then waiting out the slow start for the payoff.
activities.whyItWorks: The slow start rewards the pair who wait and watch it dance together.
activities.downTheTrack: Staying with a slow reward, which trains the patience quick apps erode.
activities.safety: Never taste the experiment glass. Use a separate cup for a real drink.

themes.bringItTogether: Across the week you fizzed, melted, froze and mixed, and every time you guessed first and then found out, which is exactly how real scientists think.

themes.title: How things move
themes.hook: Ramps, rolling, pushing, and why things fall. Guess what will happen first, then set it rolling and find out.

activities.title: The great ramp race
activities.oneLiner: How steep does it need to be to win?
activities.whatYouNeed: A big book or board, a few round things that roll, some floor space.
activities.getReady: Lean the board on a cushion to make a ramp. Clear a run at the bottom.
activities.howToDoIt: Roll something down and guess how far it goes, then make the ramp steeper.
activities.howToGuide: Let them lift the ramp higher and lower. Ask what changed each time.
activities.trySaying: "Steeper or flatter? Which one goes further, do you reckon?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a smoother floor so the roll does not stop short.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just rolls a ball down and chases it.
activities.makeHarder: An older one marks where it stops and tries to beat their own mark.
activities.builds: Changing one thing, the steepness, and reading what it does to the roll.
activities.whyItWorks: A ramp is a real problem where the floor gives you the honest answer.
activities.downTheTrack: Learning by tinkering, the hands-on sense no screen can hand over.
activities.safety: Keep heavy rolling things off toes and away from glass. Clear the run first.

activities.title: Push and stop
activities.oneLiner: Which floor makes the toy car stop first?
activities.whatYouNeed: A toy car or a smooth block, a rug, a wooden floor or tiles.
activities.getReady: Line up a spot to push from so each go starts the same.
activities.howToDoIt: Push the car the same over each surface and guess which stops it soonest.
activities.howToGuide: Let them feel the rug and the smooth floor. Ask why they feel different.
activities.trySaying: "Same push each time. Where does it stop the quickest?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Give a firmer push so the difference between floors shows up.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child pushes the car and watches it slow down.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses the order of three surfaces before testing.
activities.builds: Keeping the push the same so the floor is the only thing that changes.
activities.whyItWorks: Guessing then measuring turns a shove into a fair little experiment.
activities.downTheTrack: Setting up a fair test, the clear thinking that keeps you from being fooled.
activities.safety: Rough surfaces have more grip, so they slow a rolling thing down faster.

activities.title: Build a marble run
activities.oneLiner: Can you get the marble all the way to the bottom?
activities.whatYouNeed: Toilet rolls, cardboard, tape, a marble or a small ball.
activities.getReady: Gather the tubes and find a wall or the side of the couch to tape to.
activities.howToDoIt: Join tubes into a track that carries the marble down without it falling out.
activities.howToGuide: Let it fail and let them fix it. Do not straighten the track for them.
activities.trySaying: "Where did it fall out? What could catch it there?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the slope steeper so the marble keeps its speed.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child rolls the marble down one single tube.
activities.makeHarder: An older one adds a turn or a jump the marble has to make.
activities.builds: Making a new thing from scraps and rebuilding it until it works.
activities.whyItWorks: There are a hundred ways to lay the track and they choose their own.
activities.downTheTrack: Sticking at a fiddly build, the grit that outlasts any easy shortcut.
activities.safety: Keep marbles away from babies and toddlers who might put them in mouths.

activities.title: What falls faster
activities.oneLiner: Drop two things at once. Guess which lands first.
activities.whatYouNeed: A scrunched sock and a flat sheet of paper, then a ball and a feather.
activities.getReady: Stand somewhere safe to drop things, well clear of faces.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold two things up high, guess which lands first, then let them go together.
activities.howToGuide: Let them do the dropping and the watching. Try the paper flat then scrunched.
activities.trySaying: "Same time, or one first? What do you think?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Drop from up high so there is time to see the difference.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just drops one thing and watches it land.
activities.makeHarder: An older one scrunches the paper into a ball and guesses again.
activities.builds: Watching closely enough to catch which one hits the ground first.
activities.whyItWorks: A surprising drop makes them ask why, which is where science starts.
activities.downTheTrack: Trusting your own eyes over a guess, the check that spots a wrong answer.
activities.safety: Flat paper catches the air and floats. Scrunched up it drops like the sock.

activities.title: Swing and count
activities.oneLiner: Can you make the swing go slow, then quick?
activities.whatYouNeed: String, a small soft weight like a bean bag, a spot to hang it.
activities.getReady: Tie the weight to the string and hang it so it swings freely.
activities.howToDoIt: Pull it back, let go, and count the swings. Try a long string, then a short one.
activities.howToGuide: Let them start each swing. Count out loud together as it goes.
activities.trySaying: "Long string or short string? Which swings slower?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Make the two strings very different lengths so the change is clear.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just pushes it and watches it swing back.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses the number of swings before counting them.
activities.builds: Starting the swing themselves and running the little test their own way.
activities.whyItWorks: Counting side by side turns a swinging string into a shared game.
activities.downTheTrack: Doing it yourself and counting for real, habits a passive screen never builds.
activities.safety: Keep the swinging weight soft and clear of faces and heads.

activities.title: Domino knock down
activities.oneLiner: Set them up, tip one, and watch the whole line fall.
activities.whatYouNeed: Dominoes, blocks, or old cards or coasters stood on their edges.
activities.getReady: Clear a flat patch of floor with a bit of space around it.
activities.howToDoIt: Stand a line of them close together, then tip the first and watch it run.
activities.howToGuide: Let them space the pieces. Too far apart and the run stops, so let it.
activities.trySaying: "Closer or further apart? Guess before you tip it."
activities.ifNotWorking: Move the pieces closer so each one can reach the next.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child stands up three and knocks them with their hand.
activities.makeHarder: An older one builds a curve or a branch in the line.
activities.builds: Two of you building one line and setting it off together.
activities.whyItWorks: They design the path, so every run is a thing they made new.
activities.downTheTrack: Acting on your own plan and owning the result, quirks a screen cannot teach.
activities.safety: Each piece needs to be close enough to reach the one in front to keep it going.

themes.bringItTogether: All week you rolled, pushed, dropped and swung things, and every single time you guessed first and then set it moving to find out, which is real thinking in action.

themes.title: Magnets
themes.subtitle: the invisible pull, and what it grabs
themes.hook: There's a force you can't see, and it only grabs some things. Guess what it wants, then find out. Every magnet here is a big one, chosen because it's too large to swallow.

activities.title: The great fridge hunt
activities.oneLiner: What in the house grabs the magnet, and what shrugs it off?
activities.whatYouNeed: One large fridge magnet, a basket of safe bits like a spoon, a plastic cup, a wooden peg, a key, a sock.
activities.getReady: Gather the objects into a basket first.
activities.howToDoIt: Touch the magnet to each thing and watch what holds on.
activities.howToGuide: Let them predict before each test, and don't rush the next one.
activities.trySaying: "Do you think this one will grab?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start with something you know sticks, like a spoon.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just hunts for anything that sticks.
activities.makeHarder: An older one sorts the basket into two piles first, then checks.
activities.builds: Close looking at what pulls and what stays put.
activities.whyItWorks: Every new object in the basket is a fresh little question.
activities.downTheTrack: Noticing patterns others miss stays valuable as machines take over the routine sorting.
activities.safety: Use only large magnets that cannot be swallowed. Keep them away from mouths, and away from phones, cards and computers.

activities.title: Two piles and a guess
activities.oneLiner: Can you call it before you test it?
activities.whatYouNeed: A large magnet, ten household objects, two sheets of paper.
activities.getReady: Draw a big circle on each sheet, one for "will grab", one for "won't".
activities.howToDoIt: Guess each object's pile first, then test it and move it across if you were wrong.
activities.howToGuide: Ask why they think so, and leave the guess alone until the test.
activities.trySaying: "Guess first, then we find out."
activities.ifNotWorking: Do three objects instead of ten.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child guesses out loud and you place the object.
activities.makeHarder: An older one keeps a tally of right and wrong guesses.
activities.builds: Making a call and then testing it honestly.
activities.whyItWorks: A wrong guess isn't a fail, it's the interesting part.
activities.downTheTrack: Guess-then-check thinking is how you catch a confident answer that's actually wrong.
activities.safety: Magnets grab iron and steel, not aluminium, copper, plastic or wood. A drink can is usually aluminium, so it won't stick.

activities.title: Make a magnet fishing rod
activities.oneLiner: Build a rod and reel a catch up off the floor.
activities.whatYouNeed: A large magnet, string, a stick or wooden spoon, and steel things to catch like large spoons and steel lids.
activities.getReady: Tie the magnet to the string, then tie the string to the stick.
activities.howToDoIt: Dangle the magnet, catch the steel bits, and lift them into a bucket.
activities.howToGuide: Let them hold and aim, and step in only for the knot.
activities.trySaying: "You have a go at reeling it in."
activities.ifNotWorking: Shorten the string so the magnet is easier to aim.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child holds the magnet straight in their hand.
activities.makeHarder: An older one catches only the steel and leaves the plastic behind.
activities.builds: Making a working tool with your own two hands.
activities.whyItWorks: The child runs the whole catch, from cast to bucket.
activities.downTheTrack: Hands-on making and doing is the human edge no screen can replace.
activities.safety: Use only large magnets that cannot be swallowed. Keep the magnet and the catch away from mouths, and away from phones and cards.

activities.title: The dancing tin friend
activities.oneLiner: Make a little steel character and move it with a hidden pull.
activities.whatYouNeed: A large steel lid or spoon, tape, paper, textas, a large magnet, and a tray or shoebox lid.
activities.getReady: Decorate the lid with a paper face together.
activities.howToDoIt: Sit the friend on top of the tray, slide the magnet underneath, and watch it glide.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder together about how it moves, and take turns steering.
activities.trySaying: "Where should our friend go dancing?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a lighter object and a thinner tray.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child slides the magnet while you hold the tray.
activities.makeHarder: An older one draws a road on the tray and steers along it.
activities.builds: Turning a plain lid into something new.
activities.whyItWorks: You make and wonder side by side, sharing the steering.
activities.downTheTrack: Building things together, and caring how the other person feels, stays deeply human work.
activities.safety: Use only large magnets that cannot be swallowed, and keep the magnet well away from any phone, tablet, cards or computer.

activities.title: How many sheets before it falls?
activities.oneLiner: Slide paper behind the magnet until it can't hold on.
activities.whatYouNeed: A large magnet, a stack of paper, and the fridge or a steel door.
activities.getReady: Stick the magnet to the fridge.
activities.howToDoIt: Slide one sheet at a time behind the magnet and count until it drops.
activities.howToGuide: Let them count and keep going, even when it gets slow.
activities.trySaying: "One more sheet, let's see."
activities.ifNotWorking: Use thicker card so it drops sooner and the game moves faster.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child slides the paper while you count.
activities.makeHarder: An older one guesses the number first, then tests it.
activities.builds: Staying with a slow, fiddly job right to the end.
activities.whyItWorks: Counting to the exact drop point is testing an idea for real.
activities.downTheTrack: Patience with a long test matters when quick answers are cheap and often wrong.
activities.safety: A magnet's pull reaches through paper but fades fast with distance. That's why it lets go once the stack gets thick.

activities.title: The hidden pull hunt
activities.oneLiner: Some magnets hide where you'd never look. Can you find them?
activities.whatYouNeed: One large magnet.
activities.getReady: Nothing, just walk the house together.
activities.howToDoIt: Carry the magnet slowly near cupboard doors, the fridge seal and the pinboard, and feel where something tugs back.
activities.howToGuide: Follow their lead and wonder out loud alongside them.
activities.trySaying: "Did you feel that little tug?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Start at the fridge door seal, where the pull is strong.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child rests their hand on yours and feels the magnet move.
activities.makeHarder: An older one maps every hidden magnet they find around the house.
activities.builds: Wondering together on a shared hunt.
activities.whyItWorks: Every cupboard becomes a "what if there's one here" question.
activities.downTheTrack: Picking up a faint signal takes the kind of focus that only sharpens with practice.
activities.safety: Fridge doors and many cupboards have hidden magnetic strips or catches to hold them shut. Keep the magnet away from the TV, phones and bank cards.

themes.bringItTogether: Across the week your child looks closely, guesses out loud, builds with their hands and hunts alongside you, all while learning that an invisible pull only grabs some things and the way to know which is to test it.

themes.title: Weather
themes.subtitle: clouds, sun, rain, and reading the sky
themes.hook: The sky changes its mind all day long. Look up, guess what it'll do next, then wait and find out. Sun hats on, and always come inside when thunder rumbles.

activities.title: What's that cloud doing?
activities.oneLiner: Lie back and watch the sky change its mind.
activities.whatYouNeed: A picnic rug, sun hats, and a shady spot.
activities.getReady: Find shade and lay the rug out.
activities.howToDoIt: Watch the clouds together and describe what you see and how they drift.
activities.howToGuide: Let the quiet moments sit, and follow whatever they notice.
activities.trySaying: "What can you see up there?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Turn it into a game and find a cloud shaped like an animal.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child points and names the shapes.
activities.makeHarder: An older one watches a single cloud and describes how it changes over a few minutes.
activities.builds: Slow, patient looking at a sky that keeps moving.
activities.whyItWorks: A shifting cloud invites endless what-is-that questions.
activities.downTheTrack: Deep noticing is a human skill no feed can hand you.
activities.safety: Sun hat and shade, and never look straight at the sun.

activities.title: Read the sky, call the weather
activities.oneLiner: Guess this afternoon's weather, then find out if you were right.
activities.whatYouNeed: A window or a step outside, and sun hats.
activities.getReady: Look up at the sky together in the morning.
activities.howToDoIt: Make a weather guess for later, then head back out in the afternoon to check it.
activities.howToGuide: Ask what clues they used, and don't feed them the answer.
activities.trySaying: "What do you reckon the sky will do?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Guess just one thing, sunny or cloudy.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child picks from two little pictures you draw.
activities.makeHarder: An older one gives a reason for the guess and checks it later.
activities.builds: Making a real prediction and then checking it.
activities.whyItWorks: The sky is a puzzle that changes every single day.
activities.downTheTrack: Testing your own hunches guards you against believing the first confident answer.
activities.safety: Dark low clouds often mean rain, and high wispy ones often mean fair weather. Even the forecasters get it wrong sometimes, so a wrong guess is completely normal.

activities.title: Make a rain catcher
activities.oneLiner: Build something that measures how much rain really fell.
activities.whatYouNeed: A clear straight-sided jar or bottle, a marker, a ruler, and a safe outdoor spot.
activities.getReady: Mark lines up the side of the jar together.
activities.howToDoIt: Set it out in the open before rain, then read the level once the rain stops.
activities.howToGuide: Let them place it and read it, and help only with the marking.
activities.trySaying: "Where should we put it to catch the most?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Use a wider container so even a little rain shows.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child just checks if there's more water or less.
activities.makeHarder: An older one records the level after each rain across a week.
activities.builds: Building and reading a real measuring tool.
activities.whyItWorks: The child sets it up and checks it entirely themselves.
activities.downTheTrack: Making things that work in the real world keeps hands useful as software does more.
activities.safety: Come indoors and away from windows in thunder and lightning. Only set the gauge out when it's safe to be outside.

activities.title: Paint with the rain
activities.oneLiner: Let the rain finish your artwork for you.
activities.whatYouNeed: Paper, washable textas or a few drops of food colouring, and a covered step.
activities.getReady: Draw dots and shapes on the paper with the child.
activities.howToDoIt: Hold the paper out in light rain for a few seconds, watch the colours run and blur, then bring it in.
activities.howToGuide: Wonder together at what the rain did, and take turns holding it out.
activities.trySaying: "What do you think the rain will make?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Flick a few water drops from your fingers instead.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child watches while you hold the paper out.
activities.makeHarder: An older one plans which colours to place so the run looks best.
activities.builds: Making art with a partner you can't fully control.
activities.whyItWorks: You share the same little surprise, side by side.
activities.downTheTrack: Making something new with others stays warmly, stubbornly human.
activities.safety: Light rain only. Come inside and away from windows in thunder and lightning, and change into warm dry clothes after.

activities.title: The week of weather
activities.oneLiner: Keep a sky diary and see if a pattern turns up.
activities.whatYouNeed: A sheet of paper and some textas.
activities.getReady: Rule the paper into seven boxes, one for each day.
activities.howToDoIt: Each day, draw the weather in a box and keep it going all week.
activities.howToGuide: Remind them gently, and let them draw it their own way.
activities.trySaying: "Let's not miss a day."
activities.ifNotWorking: Do three days instead of seven.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child draws a sun or a cloud and nothing more.
activities.makeHarder: An older one notes whether their morning guess matched the day.
activities.builds: Coming back to the same small job day after day.
activities.whyItWorks: A week of records lets you check what actually happened.
activities.downTheTrack: Steady record-keeping over time beats a single snapshot, in life and in work.
activities.safety: Australian weather can swing fast, and one week won't show a full pattern, but keeping the record is the real skill here.

activities.title: A weather walk with all your senses
activities.oneLiner: What does today feel, sound and smell like?
activities.whatYouNeed: Sun hats and comfy shoes.
activities.getReady: Dress for the sky and head out together.
activities.howToDoIt: Walk slowly and notice the warmth, the wind, the smells and the sounds, and talk about each one.
activities.howToGuide: Let the child choose where you stop, and wonder alongside them.
activities.trySaying: "Can you feel which way the wind's going?"
activities.ifNotWorking: Stand still in one spot and just listen for a minute.
activities.makeEasier: A younger child names one thing they can feel.
activities.makeHarder: An older one leads the walk and picks what to notice next.
activities.builds: Tuning in to a shared moment outdoors.
activities.whyItWorks: Weather you can feel on your skin sharpens close attention.
activities.downTheTrack: Choosing where to go and what to notice builds a child who acts, not one who only watches.
activities.safety: Sun hat and shade, never look at the sun, and head home if you hear thunder.

themes.bringItTogether: Over the week your child looks up and lingers, guesses and checks, builds a real gauge, makes rainy art with you and keeps a steady diary, learning that reading the sky is wonder and testing rolled into one, always with a hat on and always inside when it thunders.
